items.h: A fifth English Schools medal for Nigel in 5 years
items.sum: Report on Belgrave's four walkers at the 1999 English Schools Championships at Peterborough, with bronze for Paul Graham, a near-miss for Laura Fryer and silver for Nigel Whorlow.
items.s: A fifth English Schools medal for Nigel in 5 years Report on Belgrave's four walkers at the 1999 English Schools Championships at Peterborough, with bronze for Paul Graham, a near-miss for Laura Fryer and silver for Nigel Whorlow. ENGLISH SCHOOLS CHAMPIONSHIPS, PETERBOROUGH 18 SEP 1999 A fifth English Schools medal for Nigel in 5 years This year the Bels had four athletes representing their County Schools. Paul Graham (Suffolk) and Stephen Whorlow (Kent) competed in the 3000m Junior Boys event. Paul went with the leaders for the first lap, but felt 'discretion was the better part of valour' and decided to drop back to a more acceptable pace and be happy with a bronze medal, rather than finishing the race early through disqualification. His decision was a wise one for he not only collected a medal but recorded his best ever time. Stephen was in no-man's land for the whole race. Not having the form to stay with the first three and far to fast for the rest, he found himself on his own for the whole race and came home in 4th place. Laura Fryer (Kent) chased the eventual winner (also from Kent) in the inter-girl's 3000m for six of the seven and half laps before tying up and dropping back. Thinking she was in a clear 2nd place, she did not see the 3rd placed girl coming home fast and was taken on the last bend. Laura signalled to her coach that she couldn't go any faster and then, out of nowhere, decided she was going for 2nd place again. She sprinted and made up a huge amount of ground over the final 25 metres, only to miss out on the silver medal by 0.17secs (which after 3 kms of racing is about half a metre.) This brought about the unusual situation in Race Walking of a photo-finish being required. Have we not heard about Laura's last minute sprints before somewere? If only she could even her pace out throughout the whole of her races she would save those watching from having near heart attacks. Nigel Whorlow (Senior Boys' 5000m) decided before the race that he was not going to suffer the ignominy of a dq as he had at the National Road Races and settled for silver medal in an uneventful race. It was his fifth English Schools medal in as many years. items.h: It's 50 and out on the A4!
items.sum: Eric Hall's report on the 50th and last Chippenham to Calne 6 miles walk on 9 October 1999, where the Belgrave team placed 9th.
items.s: It's 50 and out on the A4! Eric Hall's report on the 50th and last Chippenham to Calne 6 miles walk on 9 October 1999, where the Belgrave team placed 9th. CHIPPENHAM TO CALNE - 6 MILES, 9 OCT 1999 It's 50 and out on the A4! This was the 50th, and last, race on the A4 between the two Wiltshire market towns and it would have been nice to record a Belgrave triumph. Nevertheless it was a very nostalgic afternoon for many and it was great to see Gerry Gregory, a member in the fifties, and first winner, along with Percy Wright another Belgravian who competed in the original race. One of the organisers of this final event was Wally Emery a former member from his days in Hampshire. An almost record entry was sent on its way from Chippenham Town Hall by the lady Mayor and the field soon straggled out along the road due to the hills in that part of the world. The Belgrave contingent was led by Carl Lawton most of the way and he arrived in Calne 38th in 51.40 to be followed by Veronique Lauer who was 5th in the ladies race one second behind Carl. Next man home Andie Goudie cruised along in 46th place mindful of conserving himself for another race the next day. His 54.09 kept him just over a minute ahead of Paul King in 55th place. Next up the hill to the finish, and it was UP hill, was yours truly in 66th place (almost his age!) and a time of 56.17 to complete the scoring four who placed 9th well out of the chance of the pork pies traditionally given to the winning team. Two other veterans completed our field in the men's event, John Dunsford showing great pluck and determination to get home, followed by George Beecham as determined as ever but who was delayed in "aiding the local constabulary in their enquiries". It seems an over keen motorist had cut in right in front of a constable! For the ladies Sue Porter made a welcome appearance finishing 36th. Paul Warburton also started but was killed off by Derry Hill to become one of the very few retirements. This race has a reputation for lengthy presentations and this year was no exception. As ever the hospitality was great, changing accommodation adequate and local interest high - it is just a pity that present day conditions make the roads too hazardous for such events. The race, and the organisers, will live on in the memories of those of us who have competed, for many years. The popularity of the event was marked by the attendance of a number of past winners. Previous Belgrave winners include Gerry Gregory, Harry Churcher, Stan Vickers and Carl Lawton. It is to be hoped that plans for an alternative route using a cycle path between the two towns will come to fruition as it would be a pity not to have a race of some kind in what has always been a popular part of the country for race walking. That is not to say that a field of over 200 could be expected every year - it just goes to show that even race walkers can be sentimental at times! Eric Hall (sometime competitor!) items.h: Many old faces but numbers down in Open 7 miles race
items.sum: Eric Hall's report and results of the Belgrave Open 7 miles walk on 27 November 1999, won in a record 47:15 by Steve Hollier, with Belgrave's men 4th.
items.s: Many old faces but numbers down in Open 7 miles race Eric Hall's report and results of the Belgrave Open 7 miles walk on 27 November 1999, won in a record 47:15 by Steve Hollier, with Belgrave's men 4th. THE BELGRAVE OPEN '7', 27 NOV 1999 Many old faces but numbers down in Open 7 miles race Probably the smallest field ever faced the starter to contest this one of the oldest walking fixtures in the calendar, writes Eric Hall. Any disappointment at the size of the field was underlined by the fact that we could only muster four entrants from the nine listed on the programme. The fact that the weather was fine accounted for a fair turnout of supporters and it was good to see a number of those who had figured in the results over the years. The race was won in a new record of 47:15 by Steve Hollier who had almost a minute on Chris Cheeseman. Of those spectating the doyen must be Percy Wright who travelled from Southampton to take photographs as a basis for his caricatures of competitors which he has carried out for a number of years. From almost the same era was Dave McMullen who made his mark in so many Club teams from the immediate post war years down to the 1960s and still turns out in Vets races albeit as a half miler these days. Another making the trip from Hampshire was George Williams now involved in introducing Power Walking to those seeking a way to keep fit in the Bournemouth area. George was an international in the 1960s and still looks as lean and hungry as ever! Johnny Morris a distance walker of some renown a few years ago turned up to give the field a look over towards the end of the race. Those officiating as judges included Ray Hall and Bob Picton while it fell to Carl Lawton to rush hither and thither to ensure everything from the issue of numbers to the handing out of prizes ran smoothly. In the ladies event Laura Fryer, one of the youngest in the field, finished a very creditable 7th in 73.44. Our men's were led home by John Hall and the team placed 4th with 50 points while the under 15 boys 2 km event was won by Steve Whorlow in 11:27 with R Harris 3rd. 1, S.Hollier (W&B) 47:15 (rec); 2, C.Cheeseman (Surrey WC) 48:07; 3, D.Bearman (Steyning) 50:34; 8, J.Hall 57:40; 18, P.King 65:03; 24, D.Fotheringham 68:18; 33, G.Beacham 78:25. items.sum: George Beecham's account of the Vierdaagse four-day march at Nijmegen, its history since 1909 and his tenth consecutive visit in 1999, with a 1929 photo of Spanish soldiers taking part.
items.s: VIERDAAGSE George Beecham's account of the Vierdaagse four-day march at Nijmegen, its history since 1909 and his tenth consecutive visit in 1999, with a 1929 photo of Spanish soldiers taking part. VIERDAAGSE The Vierdaagse (four day march) otherwise known as the Nijmegen marches are the world's largest walking event and take place every July in Nijmegen, Holland. The first Nijmegen event was held ninety years ago on 1st September 1909 when 306 walkers took part. This small number of participants included ten civilians - all the rest were servicemen. On that first occasion they did not start in Nijmegen, as participants have done since 1925, but from 15 starting points nationwide. Many stories can be told about the initial years of the marches and they were not always a success. On two occasions only 44 participants entered. Yet, the organisers felt that by persevering, their efforts would eventually pay off. Now each year there are between 35,000 and 40,000 entrants from over 40 nations around the world. Many come as part of a team and these include groups from the Army, Navy, RAF, Cadets, Police, Scouts and British Telecom etc. More than one million walkers have now taken part since that first march and in 1999 the 83rd Vierdaagse was celebrated. The participants of the event are required to walk over a four-day period, starting and finishing in Nijmegen. There are three choices of distances to cover each day 50km, 40km or 30km depending on your respective age group. Each day you take a different route and all competitors start walking at 04.00am! Competitors are allowed 13 hours each day to complete their set distance. If you are unsuccessful in achieving this, unfortunately you are not given a start card for the following day. Prohibited during the marches are race walking, jogging and running. On the last day of the event, hundreds of thousands of spectators line the final 5km of the route to encourage all the walkers to finish and it is a marvellous occasion. The servicemen wear No 1 Dress Uniforms and there are many bands. All of the walkers are given bunches of flowers by the local people over that last 5km stretch, no one likes to see walkers finish without any. Upon finishing, everyone is handed a medal and these show how many years you have completed the event. On a personal note, 1999 was my 10th consecutive visit to Nijmegen to compete in the marches and I met up with a fellow Belgravian Charlie McLennan who was part of the support team for the Metropolitan Police. George Beecham Right: A squad of Spanish soldiers take part in the 1929 version of Vierdaagse. items.sum: Flashback photograph of Gordon Pirie finishing the 1961 Surrey Road Relay Championship for South London Harriers, his last race, with a note on his "The People" revelations about amateurism.
items.s: Flashback Flashback photograph of Gordon Pirie finishing the 1961 Surrey Road Relay Championship for South London Harriers, his last race, with a note on his "The People" revelations about amateurism. Flashback The last stride in the last race of an illustrious career. Gordon Pirie crosses the line in the Surrey Road Relay Championship of 9th September 1961, taking South London Harriers to victory. Gordon's time was a full two minutes faster than any one else on that day. Three weeks later "The People" ran a series of articles in which Pirie confessed to being paid to run, revealed that some of his opponents had resorted to drugs, and generally blew the lid off the cosy world of "amateur" athletics. Photo from the collection owned by Clive Shippen. The last stride in the last race of an illustrious career. items.s: Footnote Boxed filler explaining the origins of sports shoe company names such as Adidas, Puma, Asics, Mizuno, Nike, Reebok, Saucony and Walsh. Footnote Have you ever wondered where the sports shoe companies got their names? Then read on McDuff ... Brothers Rudi and Adi Dassler were initially in partnership. When they went their separate ways Adi founded a company which bears (an abbreviation of) his name and Rudi formed Puma. Asics is from the Latin anima sana in corpore sano a sound mind in a sound body. Mizuno is the family name of the company's founder, chairman and president. Nike was the Greek goddess of victory and/or (depending upon which story you belive) was derived from the names of the Japanese financial backer of the company, Nissho-Iwai, and its founder, Ian Knight. A reebok is a small, swift gazelle. Saucony (which is pronounced saw-COE-nee in Britain but SOCK-on-ee in the States) is a name given to a river near where the company has its origins. It is a Native American word for "swiftly running waters". Norman Walsh was the founder of his company. items.sum: Letter from Mark Sinclair, Marketing Manager of sponsor FILA UK, praising the club's team spirit and wishing it well for the new season, especially the Ladies Team.
items.s: Dear Belgravians, Letter from Mark Sinclair, Marketing Manager of sponsor FILA UK, praising the club's team spirit and wishing it well for the new season, especially the Ladies Team. Dear Belgravians, It gives me great pleasure to at last write something again for The Belgravian, although now as the voice of the Sponsor, FILA, and not as an athlete and member. The last time I contributed I submitted a short series of cartoons set around the much loved and missed Tom Carter, and these were included by the then editor, Mr Bill Laws. Like the Belgravian, which is by far the best club magazine I have ever seen, Belgrave continues to move on and on. As an ex-athlete, and Marketing Manager for Fila UK I am constantly reminded of what a superb example of team work the club really is. Of course, many people in the sport are envious of you. They believe that the club succeeds because of its financial security. I know, and you know, that they need to look deeper. I am old enough to remember the days where Belgrave leaped from league to league with only a handful of competitors as a result of great atmosphere, camaraderie, and hard training. And from what I have seen recently, nothing has changed except the names. The club's financial security has come from an extremely professional Team Management married to the Belgrave Team Spirit and little else. Other clubs must look harder to find out what it is that makes our club the best in the Country and one of the best in Europe. I am extremely proud of the club and FILA are proud to be involved as Sponsor. The Club embodies what club athletics must be about in this new Century. Please accept our best wishes to you all for this year, especially the Ladies Team, who are undoubtedly going through a significant stage in the club's growth and about to make history! Sincerely yours, Mark Sinclair, Marketing Manager, Fila UK Ltd. Mark Sinclair Mark Sinclair Marketing Manager, Fila UK Ltd.; ex-athlete and former member Tom Carter Tom Carter Bill Laws Mr Bill Laws former editor of The Belgravian

They help in many ways and as far as The Belgravian is concerned they have kindly purchased computer software for us which will enable your Editor to carry out a lot of the tasks that are normally done at the print shop and thus help us to keep costs down. This edition also marks another milestone in the magazine's development with a full page advertisement by David Lloyd Leisure Ltd. who are offering reduced membership to Belgrave Harriers. If you are thinking of joining a health club then get on down to the David Lloyd Club at Raynes Park - and if you haven't thought about it, maybe you should! Don't forget to tell them that you are a member of Belgrave Harriers and take your copy of the magazine with you to show that you are eligible for reduced membership. items.s: Editorial on Belgrave's growing European club competition (seniors in Group A in Madrid, juniors representing the UK) and on the club's plans to develop its women's teams, with Phil Green joining to organise IAAF Grand Prix II entries. As the Britain considers the implications of closer political and economic ties with Europe, Belgrave Harriers is strengthening its links with athletic competition on the mainland in a big way. Last summer our senior men's team won Group B of the European Champion Clubs competition in Liege, Belgium, and are now relishing the chance of taking on the giants of Group A in 2001. It will be a huge task to compete successfully against teams that are virtually national squads or sponsored by multinational companies but the dream is that one day Belgrave Harriers will become champions of Europe. At the time of writing it is believed that this year's competition will be held in Madrid on the last weekend in May. And for the first time the seniors will be joined in European competition by Belgrave's junior men's team who will also be representing the United Kingdom against the best under 20 teams from across the channel. All credit to John Powell's Team Managership that has taken our young men to this stage. As John retires to take on other roles in the sport, Paul Ireland takes over to lead our team to, we hope, even greater success. An explosion is taking place in our women's teams. UK Athletics has announced plans to reorganise certain team competitions from 2002 onwards and in particular to combine some men's and women's teams. In recognition of this, Belgrave Harriers has produced plans to meet both this developing situation and the future needs of the sport. As part of its Development Programme, Belgrave is supporting its top women members in the same way that it has supported its top male athletes. Part of this support includes help for overseas training and competition. Phil Green, well known as a team manager for the UK and for various club teams has become a Belgravian and is masterminding plans for our top male and female athletes to compete in IAAF Grand Prix II meetings. Many top class female athletes have been attracted by this programme and there is no doubt that we should be able to make a dramatic impact on women's League and Cup competition in 2001. Our aim is for our women's track & field team to reach the final of the UK Women's Jubilee Cup. And the winners of that competition will go on to compete in Europe in 2002 ... items.h: Hon. Secretary's Report to the 2000 Annual General Meeting
items.sum: Charles Henn's report to the 2000 AGM covering deaths of past presidents, a bequest, the abandoned merger with Borough of Hounslow AC, child protection policy and the club's cross-country, road, track and Olympic achievements of the year.
items.s: Hon. Secretary's Report to the 2000 Annual General Meeting Charles Henn's report to the 2000 AGM covering deaths of past presidents, a bequest, the abandoned merger with Borough of Hounslow AC, child protection policy and the club's cross-country, road, track and Olympic achievements of the year. Hon. Secretary's Report to the 2000 Annual General Meeting We heard with sadness during the year of the deaths of Charlie Jones, Frank Jarvis and Win Shepherd, who were Presidents of the Club in 1959/60,1966/67 and 1990/91 respectively, and also of Don Brown, Daye Donovan, Len Herbert and Eddie Short. The Club has been honoured by a bequest of more than £4000 under the will of Pamela Lilian Pyer, in memory of her father, Micky Pyer, who was President in 1971/72. The Committee were approached about a year ago by the Chairman of the Borough of Hounslow Athletic Club and some of his colleagues, with a view to the possible amalgamation of the two clubs. The Committee saw a number of potential advantages in amalgamation, on terms that were agreed after much discussion, though of course everything was subject to the approval of the memberships of the two clubs. In the event there was more opposition within the Borough of Hounslow club than their Chairman had expected, their proposal was withdrawn, and the Extraordinary General Meeting that your Committee had arranged provisionally was called off. The Committee are developing a child protection policy aimed to ensure that the Club discharges its responsibilities towards its younger members. Though this policy is yet to be finalised in detail - it will be suitably notified to all concerned once it has been - we envisage that there will be (1) a code of practice for coaches, team managers and others who work with Club members under 16 years of age; (2) a register of those coaches and others who have been cleared by the Club for such work after producing a letter of police clearance; and (3) a formal complaints procedure to be followed if, unhappily, it should ever become necessary. The policy will be consistent with guidance which is available nationally. The Committee believe that the Club should set up effective arrangements as soon as possible, and wish in readiness to see a Club Child Protection Officer elected by this AGM. In athletics terms, the Club has had another highly successful year. The Club team in the men's National 6-stage road relay in Sutton Park last October finished an excellent fourth in our first appearance at this event. Following the advances of recent times, Belgrave men won the Surrey Cross-Country League for the first time in twenty-eight years, by a close margin over Thames Hare & Hounds - and our under-13s were also overall winners in their age-group. Although our team was narrowly beaten into second place in the South of the Thames 'Junior' cross-country championships, Belgrave won the 'Senior' race for the third successive year. Sixth place in the South of England Cross-Country championships was followed by an excellent sixth place - and first Southern club - in the 'National': indeed, with nine to score Belgrave were fourth club. But bronze medals in the South of England 12-stage road relay in early April were followed by seventeenth place in the National race at the end of the month: it was good that we finished a team, for the first time since 1994, but too many people were unavailable for the Club to finish where it should. Belgrave's women had a good winter, too. Restored to the first division of the Surrey Cross-Country League, they finished sixth to maintain their place in it; and they won bronze medals in the Surrey Cross-Country championships. It was very good to see a group of our women make up their minds to a good performance in the London Marathon, and after preparing together and running as a team secure the bronze medals - indeed they were the first women's team to close in, and all three scorers recorded considerable personal bests. In track and field athletics our men's team were once again champions of the First Division of the British Athletics League, for the fourth year running; and a first-rate performance in winning the second division match of the European Champion Clubs Cup meant this country's promotion, so that Belgrave as national champions once again will take part next year in the first division match. However, the dependence of any club on getting people to turn out - something especially difficult, perhaps, in an Olympic year - was illustrated by our lapse to fourth place domestically in the Gold Cup. Our team in Division One of the Men's Southern League, always liable to be 'raided' at short notice to supply our British League team, found the going hard this year but have retained their place. The Club's women finished in the middle of Division Three of the Southern Women's League. Our under-20 men's team, after winning the Southern Premier Division of the National Junior League, went on to win the national final at Birmingham last weekend; and in the National Junior League Grand Prix final, held in parallel, Tim Abeyie and Scott Thompson finished first and second. Sadly, however, Belgrave have lost their place in the Southern Premier Division of the Young Athletes' League: in the young age-groups, of course, a high proportion of any team moves up into the next age-group each year, so that clubs' standards are volatile, and very vulnerable to any lapse in recruitment. As always, there have been many outstanding individual achievements. To mention just two individual races: we have seen Dwain Chambers beat Maurice Green, and Chris Rawlinson has established a new world best performance in the, admittedly unusual, 300 metres hurdles event. Eight members of the Club have been selected to represent Great Britain in the Olympic Games that begin next week at Sydney, nearly a fifth of the men's athletics team: Sean Baldock, Darren Campbell, Ben Challenger, Dwain Chambers, Justin Chaston, Matt Douglas, Phillips Idowu and Chris Rawlinson; and Brendan Reilly has been picked for Ireland. Let me end on a different and longer-term note. The Club's success also depends on Club members being willing to give up time and energy to the jobs that have to be done - the team managers, the coaches, the match officials, those who organise social events for everyone's enjoyment and to generate income, those who maintain this Hall, those who manage the Club itself, and those who help in other ways. We owe all of them our thanks. Without them the Club would not survive, let alone flourish, and without them and people like them in other clubs there would indeed be no organised athletics in this country. For some of these functions it would be an understatement to say that more help is needed. C.H. Henn, 14th September 2000. C.H. Henn C.H. Henn Hon. items.h: Back home again! The Millennium Arena, Battersea Park
items.sum: Eric Hall's history of Belgrave's use of the Battersea Park track from 1921 to its reopening as the Millennium Arena, opened by Tessa Sanderson on 1st June 2000, with a photo of the opening day party.
items.s: Back home again! The Millennium Arena, Battersea Park Eric Hall's history of Belgrave's use of the Battersea Park track from 1921 to its reopening as the Millennium Arena, opened by Tessa Sanderson on 1st June 2000, with a photo of the opening day party. Back home again! The Millennium Arena, Battersea Park Eric Hall reminds us of previous incarnations of our home track Now that we have access once again to what has been the Club's track home, on and off, for many years some members have been recalling earlier times and other tracks on that site. One was even heard to remark of the brand new pristine surface that it would probably be all right once the cinders had been spread over it and it had been well churned up after a storm or two! It seems possible that we first used a track in Battersea Park as long ago as 27th December 1921 for the traditional Boxing Day handicaps. In those days it was a cinder track of three laps to the mile in much the same area as the present one but going out towards the grass banking by the main road. Also in those days competitors were treated to the joy of running through the fumes belted out by Battersea Power Station if there was a down draught at the wrong time! Early in 1922 the Secretary was instructed to write to the London County Council to seek better training and changing facilities. Around the same time it was decided to use St John's Hall, Wimbledon, for winter training so this period can be seen as pivotal to our activities. At a Committee Meeting on 2nd January 1923 it was reported that no action had been taken by the L.C.C. as to erecting dressing accommodation at Battersea Park and it was decided that the Hon. Secretary should endeavour to obtain further information on this matter. Two months later a letter was received from the L.C.C. noting that the track was now available for use & that the question of a dressing room was under consideration! By April the changing accommodation had been settled as the Club was requesting that a notice board be allowed! Sounds familiar? In June 1923 Mr R.W. Ricketts suggested that the British Olympic Council be written to and requested to approach the London County Council to reserve the enclosure at the track in Battersea Park for field events and not to set up cricket pitches as then suggested. Nothing further is recorded about this initiative. At the same meeting a letter from the L.C.C. granting permission to erect a marquee was read and action in this matter was left in the hands of a sub-committee and the decision was taken that the marquee should remain until the end of September. Prior to the use of Battersea Park the Club had used the Price's Candle Co. sports ground at Earlsfield for a number of years and as this was a grass track the Committee noted that adjustments would have to be made to handicap marks as cinder tracks were faster. Among those with early memories of the track was Past President the late Win Shepherd. She recalled being taken along by her father, Dick Savage, also a Past President. She also believed that her grandfather actually worked in the Park and came home with news of the creation of an athletic track. Among others who were familiar with the track from their early days are Arthur Penny and Bill Lucas. At the outbreak of the Second World War Battersea was requisitioned and so the Club moved, in 1940, to Tooting Bec for the duration - and a little longer. Even this move did not break Win Shepherd's connection as her husband, Past President Dave Martin-Shepherd, was an active member of the Home Guard who manned an AA gun on the site! By 1954 the Club was able to return but by now it was a standard track albeit of imperial measurement - that is four laps to the mile! Eventually even a hammer cage appeared after the threatened prosecution of a Club thrower for demonstrating his art without adequate protection of other users. Various refurbishments and conversions took place in the 1960s when it was made metric. Further improvements were made in 1983 when a Spurtan BS synthetic track was laid. The old track was closed in May 1999 and we now have a new two storey pavilion, a covered stand alongside the home straight, electric timing and an upgraded, very soft, Polytan WS surfaced track consisting of 8 lanes. The total cost of over £2.6m was jointly funded by Wandsworth Council and a Lottery Sports Award. Now officially known as the Millennium Arena it was opened by Tessa Sanderson on 1st June. To many it will still be known as the Battersea Park Track. As a final note there is no truth in the rumour that the Club demanded completed membership applications from the Red Devil team who helped in the launch of the Capital Cities Meeting - perhaps we ought to have done so as they looked a fairly useful group of high flyers! Sorry about that. The assembled dignitaries of Wandsworth Council join Belgravians, Track Staff, Surrey representatives and Tessa Sanderson on official opening day - 1st June 2000. items.sum: Profile of new club President John Jeffery, from Metropolitan Police middle-distance runner to Belgrave team manager and committee member, with his portrait.
items.s: No ordinary man ... Profile of new club President John Jeffery, from Metropolitan Police middle-distance runner to Belgrave team manager and committee member, with his portrait. John Jeffery, President of Belgrave Harriers 2000-2001 No ordinary man ... When one finds out that John Jeffery "only" became a Belgrave Harrier in 1992, January 20th to be precise, it seems quite impossible that this man, who is so much a part of every aspect of our Club, can have been with us for less than a decade. And of course it is impossible because in actual fact he has been a part of the Belgrave scene since 1963. As a 19 year-old, John came to live south of the Thames for the first time to become a Metropolitan Police officer. He had been a member of Southgate A.C. in North London. Now, as a police officer in 'L' Division, he fell in with one of the hardest working group of middle-distance runners in the south-east, all of them police officers and forming part of a formidable track & field team - the Metropolitan Police A.A.C. Among them, Andy Norman was a 440 yards man who was turning his talents towards coaching and team management, John Backley (father of Steve, today's champion spearman) ran half-miles and Dave Prior was a redoubtable competitor over 1 mile and beyond. John often trained at Battersea Park and it was not long before Tom Carter, with his own squad of runners working out at Battersea, approached him with a view to signing him up. John was interested but fully committed to the Metropolitan Police team. He promised Tom that "one day" he would. The intervening years saw John blossom as a middle-distance runner. He became British Police Champion at 400m, 800m, 1500m and cross-country. He represented the Southern Counties and A.A.A. and set personal bests of 49.6 for 400m, 1:50.2 for 800m, 3:49.8 for 1500m, 49:50 for 10 miles - which he regards as probably his best ever run over any distance - and even ran a marathon, towards the end of his racing days, in 2:36. He remained close to our Club, always prepared to spend a bit of time with anyone looking for advice on running and training - and for a while entered into a role of official Belgrave coach at Battersea until, during lean times in the '70s, we found we had very few middle-distance track runners left who wanted coaching! He had a fine athletic career by any standard but John was one of that rare breed who continued to pour his talent and experience into the sport when his own running days had passed. He became the Southern Counties Administrator, a post he held for six years. He took on roles as English and British Team Manager, travelling all over the globe. He coached; he judged; he organised. Was there any aspect of our sport not tackled by John. True to his word, when his Metropolitan Police days were over, John became a Belgravian. As we have already learned he is not one to do things by halves and becoming a Belgravian, for him, meant taking on responsibility. As Leo Coy, highly successful joint British League team manager, stepped aside to return to his native Ireland, John walked right into the breach. Leo and Bill Laws had taken our track & field team on a white-knuckle ride from Southern League to the very top of the British League. It would take no ordinary man to fill Leo's shoes - but John is far from ordinary. All we can say is that the combination of Bill and John is, today, one of the toughest partnerships in our sport and between them they have consolidated our position as Britain's top male track & field team. We re-organised our club administration: John was in there giving support. He became a member of our Committee and one of our key men in "Public Relations & Sponsorship". From time to time as the governing bodies and administrators of our sport back themselves from one corner into another, John continues to be approached with offers of high ranking positions in Athletics but he has become an integral part of the Belgrave management team and continues to pack as much hard work for the Club into his days as is humanly possible. Is there any surprise that we welcome John into the highest office in our Club - President of Belgrave Harriers. items.sum: Report of the Annual Dinner Dance on 25 November 2000 welcoming John Jeffery as President, with the club trophy winners and the 1960s distance runners present.
items.s: Members and guests celebrate at Annual Club Dinner Report of the Annual Dinner Dance on 25 November 2000 welcoming John Jeffery as President, with the club trophy winners and the 1960s distance runners present. Members and guests celebrate at Annual Club Dinner At the Annual Dinner Dance at the Preston Cross Hotel held on 25 November 2000 to celebrate the 113th year of the Club, around 130 members and their guests formally welcomed John Jeffery as the new President of Belgrave Harriers. Special Guests were Mark Sinclair of FILA UK - kit sponsors to Belgrave Harriers, Mike Winch - representing the AAA of England, and John Thresher - until very recently the Chief Executive of Athletics Canada and a Belgrave Harrier himself since 1957. Among other notables present was 92 year-old Arthur Penny - 1934 Empire Games 6 miles Champion. Toastmaster was Past President and 1948 Olympic representative Bill Lucas, DFC and the function was organised by yet another Past President, Ted Pallant. The Club's major individual trophy winners were announced. The "Tommy Green" Cup for the best performance by a male Belgravian during the preceding year went to Darren Campbell for his run in the Olympic 200 metres final where he won the Silver Medal. The "Centenary" Cup, the equivalent award for women went to Helen Alsop née Maskrey who led the Belgrave team to the bronze medals in the AAA Marathon, held in conjunction with the 2000 London Marathon. Nineteen year-old Scot Thompson was presented with the "Bill Merryman" Trophy for the Young Belgravian of the Year. Discus thrower Scot had played a huge role in the Club's successful campaign to win the National Junior League during the past summer. The Dinner gives the chance for many Belgravians to renew old friendships and a great many of the Club's outstanding distance runners from the 1960s were present: Gerry North (National Cross Country Champion), Geoff North (AAA 3 miles Champion), Tony Fairclough, Lionel Mann, Alan Black - and of course John Thresher himself who ran an outstanding 13:49.0 for 5,000 metres as long ago as 1965 - on "cinders". items.sum: Tributes to newly elected Life Members Rex Bale, field judge and Minutes Secretary, and Tony Fairclough, 1960s distance runner turned Grade II track official.
items.s: Newly Elected Life Members Tributes to newly elected Life Members Rex Bale, field judge and Minutes Secretary, and Tony Fairclough, 1960s distance runner turned Grade II track official. Newly Elected Life Members Rex Bale Rex Bale Has been a Belgravian for 24 years, since 19th July 1976. We are always so pleased to find someone who will turn up at an athletics meeting to help but Rex does far more than that - when he attends he takes responsibility for whatever needs to be done. He is respected throughout Surrey as a Field Event Judge and is often called upon to be Field Referee. Come to any of our home matches and the odds are that Rex will have been there since half past ten or eleven o'clock, sweeping the long jump runways, shifting the sand forward in the pits and calibrating the high jump and pole vault stands. Athletes start arriving from noon onwards and then it's a case of weighing in the throwing implements before the competitions start. Actual judging follows, together with the checking and signing of results cards. At the end of the meeting as competitors drift off home, some seven hours since his tour of duty started, Rex will still be there collecting up the equipment that has been left all over the arena and for which he signed earlier. He is one of that most valuable band that are prepared to travel to away fixtures on our behalf - women's fixtures, men's or youngsters'; Birmingham, Southend, wherever necessary to help the Club fulfil its obligations. It doesn't stop at officiating either, for Rex is Minutes Secretary for our main Committee. We deal with so much business these days that it is imperative that the records of our meetings are correctly documented and Rex does this admirably. He also acts as our Press Officer for Winter events and is our man at Battersea, very much involved in keeping an eye on what is going on there; he played a vital role as the track was recently being developed. Like many another who does a fine job no matter what he turns his hand to, Rex is in demand outside our own club and he is Officials Secretary for Veterans A.C. All this and he still enjoys his running. Tony Fairclough Tony joined Belgrave in 1959 as one of 'Tom's lads' a group coached by the late Tom Carter and Bob Taylor, which included Jackie Hampshire, Dave Cocks, Alan Morrison, Alan Mead and Chris Steer. He first appeared for the Club in the Belgrave Youths road relay in 1959 and went on to a most successful career at Club and County level. His athletic achievements include:- - 14th in the Surrey Youths' Cross Country, 1961. - Gaining a Surrey Vest and placing 16th in the Junior Inter-Counties of 1963. - Setting a New Club record on Stage 6 of the London-Brighton Relay, 1963 (record still stands today!) - 4th in the Surrey Junior Cross Country, 1964. - 3rd in the Southern Junior Cross Country, 1964. - 5th in the National Junior Cross Country, 1964. - 19th in the National Junior Inter-Counties Cross Country, 1964. - Being ranked 7th overall in the National Junior Cross Country rankings and gaining an ECCU Vest. - 36th in the National Senior Cross Country, 1967, and being awarded a Club Honours Badge. - Becoming a regular member of Surrey CC and Belgrave London-Brighton Relay teams. - Winning Club Championships at Junior 5 miles CC, Senior 6 miles track, 10 miles CC and 5.75 miles Road Race. Tony was a Team Managers delight; uncomplicated, reliable and always giving 100% effort. His quiet and unassuming disposition belied the tenacity he applied to his running. When his competitive career drew to a close, Tony took to officiating, becoming a Grade IV Track Judge in 1990. He has now 'risen through the ranks' to become a highly respected Grade II official. He attends most of our 'home' meetings at Battersea alongside his wife Gillian who is a Grade II Field Events Judge, but does not confine his activities only to the track. During the winter season he appears at cross country and road fixtures, not only for Belgrave but also for County and SEAA events. Although living at Gillingham in Kent, Tony has been a most loyal Club member over the years and a great ambassador, not only for our Club but for our sport in general. items.s: Don E. Brown 1911-2000 Obituary of race walker and walking judge Don E. Brown (1911-2000), with an archive photo of a 1930s walk match at Battersea whose identifications the editor asks readers to help confirm. Obituaries Don E. Brown 1911-2000 We have learned recently of the death of Don Brown in February last. Don E. Brown is noted as a new member in the August/September 1931 issue of the Belgravian. He was one of a batch of notables to whom a welcome was extended at that time. Others were A.G. Bruce; A.E. Taylor; H.W. Shields and the Churcher brothers, Charlie and Harry. Don's name was linked with the latter in race results in the late 1930s. Just turned 20 when he joined us, he soon became a force to be reckoned with in the shorter distance walks. The next issue of the magazine noted that "D.E. Brown impressed in his first race as likely to do very well in the future". He finished 22nd in the Opening 5 mile event of the 1931/32 season with the Churcher brothers among those in front of him. He maintained steady progress throughout the next few seasons in the various Open 7s. moving out to 10 miles he was 6th in the RWA "Junior" in 1933 and was second member of the team led home by Harry Churcher and completed by Alf Harley. In 1934 Don was third in the AAA's two mile track walk in 13 mins 58 secs., the fastest time then by a Belgravian. Elected Road Captain at the next AGM - no mean feat for one so young - he led by example in both inter-club and Open events and gained his Surrey colours. The next year he improved to second place in the AAA's two miles behind the great A. A. Cooper in the "amazingly fast time of 13 mins 53.8 secs." Two years later Don was third - behind Cooper yet gain. At that time it was said that Cooper was the bane of every track walker and both Harry Churcher and Don had to give him best on a number of occasions despite recording quite exceptional times. A quieter time followed in the years up to the outbreak of War but even so he finished 13th in the Belgrave Open 7 which indicates that he had great natural ability and although he was only in the "C" team that day they beat the "A" team to take the scratch prizes! He was also noted as a possible for the 1940 Olympic Games. As with so many other races those Games did not take place and the events of September 1939 blighted the careers of many members, Don included. He wrote in 1944 to say that despite a posting in the Sussex Weald he was unable to train. Post war Don became a highly respected walking judge, a familiar figure at all major races and in the years from 1956 to 1960 he was a frequent visitor to Battersea Park where he did much to assist Stan Vickers and myself in our careers. Don took lap times but made it a rule never to disclose them until the end of the evening. Encouragement was given in a quiet, calm, gentlemanly, manner which he always seemed to apply in any situation. In my mind's eye I still see him at the 200 metre mark advising us when necessary but ever mindful that we had our own views on training and racing programmes. He was a man to be listened to and we appreciated his opinions. He also played an active part in pacing us round Wimbledon Common by cycling at a steady 8 mph with Stan on one side of the rear of the bike and me on the other for 12 miles a session. If you think that sounds easy just try it sometime! With his concentration on style, of which I am told he was a great exponent, he presented the Club with a silver salver to be awarded annually to the best stylist in the Club 2 mile championship. No one was more delighted than Don when Stan Vickers achieved such great heights in so many races culminating in the bronze medal in the Rome Olympics 1960. A great Belgravian who was walking at the "wrong" time, so far as the standard of competition is concerned, he nevertheless gave of his best whether as a competitor, judge, advisor or friend. items.s: Win Shepherd 1925-2000 Obituary of Win Shepherd (1925-2000), race walker with London Olympiads, the club's first Ladies Secretary and first Lady President; it names her husband here as Dave Shepherd, President 1962-63 (page 5 calls him Dave Martin-Shepherd). Win Shepherd 1925-2000 Win Shepherd, who died on Sunday 27th August in her 75th year, was the first ever Lady President of Belgrave Harriers, being awarded that honour for the year 1990-91. She had been associated with the club since a toddler. Her father, Dick Savage, had been President in 1944-46 and her late husband Dave Shepherd was also President in 1962-63. Win became interested in Race Walking at the age of fifteen but as there was no ladies section of the club in those days she became a member of London Olympiads. Win was "Olympiads" club champion on three occasions, Surrey champion for three years and while representing her county in the Inter-Counties won and was placed second four times. Twice she was a member of the champion National Road Walk team. In later years she was also a respected member of another top South London club, Selsonia Ladies A.C. With her mother, Win organised the refreshments at Belgrave Hall for some nine years and when a ladies section was formed in 1976 she immediately became a full member and the club's first Ladies Secretary. She had been an honorary member for many years beforehand. Win assisted in the running of all sorts of athletics meetings from youngsters' Thameside Leagues to County Championships, generally working on the results or organising the presentation of trophies. She always had a word of encouragement for the athletes and they in turn respected her as someone who had spent her whole life involved in the sport we love. Our condolences go to Win's brother Richard, a staunch Belgrave Harrier himself. items.sum: Obituary of Frank Jarvis (1907-2000), Metropolitan Police officer, road walker, Centurion and Belgrave President from 1966, with a photo of the 1967 track and field team he presided over.
items.s: Frank Jarvis (1907-2000) Obituary of Frank Jarvis (1907-2000), Metropolitan Police officer, road walker, Centurion and Belgrave President from 1966, with a photo of the 1967 track and field team he presided over. Obituaries Frank Jarvis (1907-2000) It is with much sadness that we have to announce the death from pneumonia of Frank Jarvis aged 93, following a short spell in hospital. Frank, our oldest member, beating Arthur Penny by just a few months, was born in Hounslow on 12 March 1907, the eldest of three brothers. His father, a regular Grenadier Guardsman, was killed in action in the 1914 War and because of this Frank was unable to complete his education, having to leave school at an early age in order to help support his family. This is hard to reconcile to the man we came to know in later life who was literate, well read and knowledgable about most things and in fact was said to have inherited a silver tongue from his mother, although he claimed it came from kissing the blarney stone In 1921 Frank nearly became a member of Thames Valley Harriers when invited by that club to join them after a promising showing in a schoolboy cross-country race. But Frank was already involved in the Scouting movement and not ready to participate in another pastime. In years to come he was to play a part in the formation of the Rover Scouts. In 1928 he joined the Metropolitan Police and for 10 years served with 'C' Division at Vine Street station in London's West End. He then transferred to the information Room at New Scotland Yard, where he served throughout the war and until he retired in 1959. On leaving the Police he joined the Aliens Department of the Home Office. With his usual enthusiasm and efficiency he became a noted authority on immigration law, much in demand by the courts from whom he received an official letter of commendation for his work in this field. On joining the Police he soon became a member of the M.P.A.A. cross country team and was also a keen boxer. He took up training with the road walkers of Belgrave Harriers to develop his stamina, joining us in 1935. His interest in this new event became so strong that he soon gave up running and boxing. He was a tremendous team man. On one occasion he met with an accident at the 20 mile point in a 25 mile race, resulting in a badly cut foot. His team mates were well placed and rather than drop out and let them down, he kept going to close in the team and help them to third place. A regular competitor in the Police Barking to Southend (36 miles) road race there are two incidents associated with it that Frank always recalled. He claimed to be the only competitor in the history of the race to be pulled out for 'lifting' and the other was on a hot day when a well wisher threw a bucket of cold water over him. Unfortunately his shoes dried out like iron, and he had to be brought home in an ambulance and was off work for two weeks In 1955 he entered the London to Brighton and back (100 miles), successfully completing the course in 24 hours to become a Centurion. 1958 saw him become Hon. Secretary of the RWA Southern Area, a post he held for many years, he also became Belgrave's Assistant Hon Secretary, Walking Secretary, and Surrey County's Walking Team Manager. On retiring from active competition he served as an official at many events and travelled abroad as a team manager. Frank always claimed that one of his proudest moments came in 1966, when he was elected President of Belgrave. Looking back we can now see that Frank's Presidency came at one of those pivotal moments in our club. When he became President Belgrave had seen no track or field success to speak of for very many years. This was a period just before the formation of the leagues that we are now used to. “I feel convinced,” he said, “that if the Club was to win ONE trophy, this victory would lead to others.” His club duly rose to the task and during his term of office was victorious in the ‘Jack Lewis Trophy’, the Club's first major win for 11years. Within weeks they won another even more prestigious event, the ‘HG.Brockman Trophy’. The road to the success that we see today had been started out upon. In 1974 Frank was made president of the Road Walking Association and in 1974 President of Surrey County AA. From his first marriage in 1928 Frank had a son Paul and a daughter, Ann. Unfortunately this marriage was dissolved after 19 years, a victim of the war. He then married Hilda a charming lady who sadly died suddenly, again after 19 years of wedlock. It was then some 20 odd years ago that he married Val, with whom he spent the remaining years of his life; they were a devoted and loving couple. To Val, Paul and Ann we send our deepest condolences. items.sum: Obituary of Glasgow-born distance runner W.E. 'Bill' Kerr (1932-2000), with Clive Shippen's memories of his London to Brighton Relay runs, his best track performances 1961-68 and a photo of him handing over to Charlie Dabbs in 1965.
items.s: W.E. “Bill” Kerr 1932 - 2000 Obituary of Glasgow-born distance runner W.E. 'Bill' Kerr (1932-2000), with Clive Shippen's memories of his London to Brighton Relay runs, his best track performances 1961-68 and a photo of him handing over to Charlie Dabbs in 1965. Obituaries W.E. “Bill” Kerr 1932 - 2000 Sadly we have to announce the death of Bill Kerr on the 15th December 2000, from a sudden heart attack , aged 68 years. Bill was born in the Springburn area of Glasgow where his father was a Shipwright. In his early years he did very well at school where he was known as a 'bit of a whiz kid' for his general knowledge. Following his school years he became an apprentice on the railway, but this career was cut short following an accident when the wheel of a steam engine dropped onto his hand, leaving him with the loss of mobility in some of his fingers for the rest of his life. In Scotland Bill ran for Victoria Park A.A.C, and later on the Anglo Scottish Athletic Club. However, seeking pastures new, it was in the early 1960s that Bill came south and burst upon the Belgrave scene, going on to carve himself a lifelong niche in the hearts of many of his team mates and training partners of that time. He was a great acquisition to the Club when we badly needed one. It is most significant that since hearing of his untimely death, the underlying memory that many of his contemporaries recall was that he was such a likeable, indeed loveable fellow. One who will always be remembered for his singular sense of humour and that mischievous look in his eyes when he related a story. Perhaps Bill's style and character, as well as his athletic ability, can best be illustrated by recalling the following anecdotes relayed to me by Clive Shippen on hearing the sad news. Clive writes:- “I well remember going to Belgrave Hall in March 1961 for the ‘five and three-quarters’ road trial - a big race in those days as, generally, the first 12 were selected to carry our colours in the prestigious London to Brighton Relay which was sponsored by the News of the World. An unfamiliar face was amongst the usual crowd of nervous runners. He had been brought along by Charlie Walker and was introduced to me as Bill Kerr, a Scotsman. Straight away he struck me as being an affable fellow with a sense of humour already apparent, and he was given permission to compete as a guest. He was a relaxed runner with a long loping stride and he floated along just behind the leaders for most of the race. When he was sure of his way to the finish he eased ahead for a very surprising win. As you can imagine, he had a membership form in his hand before he had barely recovered his breath! Bill was selected for the long stage 9 of the National April 1961 race. He was not familiar with the race logistics so when the Stage 9 coach dropped off it's 20 competitors and then drove straight on to the end of the stage Bill realised that his nice new Belgrave vest, complete with attached numbers, had gone with it! I well remember a very agitated Jimmy Green (Editor of Athletics Weekly) running up to me saying 'There's an unknown runner up ahead running in an un-numbered white vest. He took over from Jack Brown so he must be one of your's. Who the hell is he? I can't recognise him. You realise he is likely to get you disqualified'. My heart sank. Somehow we managed to get ahead of the race and notify the judges of Bill's name and number. We were not penalised, and it was an auspicious start for Bill's career with Belgrave. Bill's best London to Brighton run was in the National event of April 1962 when he recorded 6th fastest time on the long stage 9 with only Kilby, Bullivant, Craig, Freary and Tulloh (all internationals) being faster. What is more he achieved that back in 14th place - one of our bad years. Bill was very easy going. Nothing rattled him. Perhaps he was too easy going. His sense of humour endeared him to all. On training runs he had a habit of plucking leaves from trees and singing little ditties; alright on training runs, but very occasionally he would do so in races - very disconcerting to the other competitors! His laid-back, easy going manner did sometimes produce anxiety in team managers. The team for the South of Thames Senior at Maidenhead in 1962 met at Paddington Station. With just 15 minutes to go before departure Bill ambled up saying, 'I'm starving, I must get something to eat'. No sign of nerves there! I suggested that he grab a sandwich to eat on the train. With 4minutes to departure he had still not arrived at the carriage so I rushed to the station buffet fearing there must have been a mishap of some sort. Bill was casually cleaning up a plate of pie and chips! He looked up at me with that mischievous smile and said 'What's the fuss?' " Bill gained a AAA vest in 1962 and went on to become a Middlesex track champion Professionally Bill worked, in turn, for the Civil Service; the Anglo Iranian Oil Company as a Project Clerk ,and in latter years as a Processing Clerk for BT. Among his interests can be listed cooking, gardening a love of the music of Peggy Lee and Frank Sinatra and, when away from athletics, hockey. In 1970 he met Eileen. They were married in 1971, setting up home first in Streatham then Sittingbourne, Kent, before settling down in Caterham where son Fraser was born in 1978. In 1963 Bill ran in the Scottish National cross country championships and gained his International Vest by finishing 6th. However after the race was over he heard one of his friends bemoaning his fate at having “missed out again” by finishing 7th. Whereupon Bill calmly said, “that's OK you can have my place,” and gave up his Vest in favour of his friend. Such was the character of the man we will affectionately remember as Bill Kerr To Eileen, and Fraser, (now studying physics at Oxford University) we extend our deepest condolences Gordon Biscoe Bill's best track performances 1961 – 1m 4:12.8; 3km 8:21.4; 2m 8:55.0; 3m 14:04.2. 1962 – 1m 4:11.8; 2m 9:07.6; 6m 29:19.4. 1963 – 1m 4:11.6; 3km 8:05.4; 2m 8:44.6; 3m 13:46.8; 6m 29:14.2. 1964 – 2m 9:01.6. 3m 13:59.2. 1965 – 1m 4:12.8; 2m 8:53.6; 3m 13:56.8. 1966 – 2m 9:17.0; 5km 14:50.0. 1967 – 1m 4:23.8; 2m 9:03.4; 3m 14:25.8. 1968 – 1m 4:14.6; 2m 9:01.6; 3m 13:55.8; 6m 31:20. items.s: J.E.C. Rutland Obituary note for former member Jack Rutland, a 1930s walker who was 2nd in the inaugural National 10 miles walk championship in 1947. Members Near and Far J.E.C. Rutland Since the last issue we have heard of the death of a former member Jack Rutland. Jack joined us in the early 1930s as a walker and soon made his mark over the shorter distances. He was a member of our National "Junior" winning team in 1936 and put up a number of noteworthy times before the war. War service in the army, mainly in Wales found him linking with fellow Belgravian Percy Wright to foster the sport. He placed 2nd to Harry Churcher in the inaugural National 10 miles championship in 1947 and was named as an Olympic "possible". Work however intervened and due to a loss of form he was not selected for the 1948 Games although a member of our National winning team that year. He remained a stalwart for a few years putting up good times over all distances until 1952 when pressures from work and family commitments intervened. J.E.C. Rutland J.E.C. items.h: It's a small world on the wide web
items.sum: Stories of former members who have rediscovered the club through the internet, from a New Zealand book dealer and an expatriate in Virginia to old members in Tokyo, California and South Africa.
items.s: It's a small world on the wide web Stories of former members who have rediscovered the club through the internet, from a New Zealand book dealer and an expatriate in Virginia to old members in Tokyo, California and South Africa. It's a small world on the wide web Coincidence is a marvellous thing, writes Eric Hall. "Having searched for many years for another copy of a book lent to a 'friend', and not returned, the final resort was to try the 'web'. For those who forecast that the internet will replace book publishing in due course this may seem an odd way of doing things but this time it was a success on two grounds. The main site for such items was found to be in the US (where else?) and after a very brief search a copy of the long lost volume was located at a reasonable price - not in the US but in New Zealand. Having searched most of the secondhand shops in those islands only a year or so ago this seemed strange but what was to follow was even stranger. The transaction was done and in a few days the book arrived in deepest Essex. Being so grateful to have found a copy after so long I decided to e-mail the sender with my heartfelt thanks. As the book was about walking training I told him of my connection with the sport and of the fact that I knew the late Norman Read the 1956 gold medallist. Back came a reply to the effect that the dealer in NZ did a bit of jogging now but had run in the UK back in the mid '70s. He said that it was a small world and added that he belonged to a club over here by the name of Belgrave Harriers! My reply was to the effect that he had no idea just how small a world it really was and as his shop was in Christchurch it might be that he knew of Paul or Peter Coughlan. Back came a reply to say that not only did he know the two gentlemen but that he had seen Peter that very afternoon and he sent his regards to all those he met this last year. In addition the book seller, Glenn Hazard, sent his regards to those who remember him and his epic run in the London to Brighton road run back in the mid seventies." A long time British expatriate sat in his Virginia, USA, home watching TV. Some 30 years previously he had joined the British Army, serving for nine years. Home after that had been, at various times, Perth (Australia), the Middle East (Oman), Malaysia, Paris, the Caribbean, but eventually he settled down in Berryville, Virginia, in the Shenandoah Valley near the Blue Mountains. He runs his own telecommunications company and still travels the world on business but here he was sitting at home watching athletics on American TV when the commentator mentioned that one of the athletes in shot competed for Belgrave Harriers in the UK. Turning to his wife, he mentioned that he too had run for that club as a young man. Memories stirred and it was but a short step from there to switching on the computer and surfing the net to see if the club had a web-site. And there it was ... news ... pictures ... and quite a few names among the contact names that he remembered from earlier days. E-mails followed and before long, on his next trip through the UK, Tony Brooks our one time track & field captain turned up to watch a cross country match and visit Belgrave Hall. It was great to see him and there is even talk about a possible retirement to live in the UK in a few years time. Tony supplied the team photograph that appears on page 9 of this magazine. Aussie John Dawson picked us up from Tokyo where he is now living and working. He ran with us while still a Junior in the mid-1990s. John went on to clock 1:50 for 800 metres and 48.1 when he returned to Australia. He has struggled with injuries for the past three years but has also qualified as a coach. "I fondly remember my times at Belgrave," he says, "and hope that one day I'll be able to return to England to compete again in claret and gold." John sends his best wishes to all and looks forward to returning to London one day. Frazer Hazlett has also got in touch. Frazer worked hard to get into our British League team but was another who had a few injury problems. He has turned to Triathlon where he is doing very well - and now lives in Southern California. Harold Hutchinson competed for the Club in 1936-38 in the sprint hurdles and pole vault. Harold's granddaughter got in touch with us when they found our web-site and now Harold is the proud owner of a club tie that brings him back many memories. Michael Peacock has e-mailed us from South Africa. He recently ran 49.37 for 400 metres in a pre-season meeting and is hoping to do well in his forthcoming season. He sends his regards to coach Bob Bridges and his old training group, especially Nick Molloy, Dotun Akinbogun, Richard David, Richard Mcmillan, Joe Panton and James Hilston; also to John Jeffrey, Mike Small, Patricia and Alan Mead and of course his good friend Past President Ted Pallant. Accounting studies will keep him busy for the next couple of years but he hopes to return to the UK and wear a Belgrave vest again. Finally we received communication from a gentleman researching his family history. His grandfather and great-grandfather had both been Belgrave Harriers and he had found us on the web: "Did we have any information regarding them?" Did we! Great-grandfather was Edwin Gordon, Past President and one time Mayor of New Malden; his Great Aunt was Elsie, who is remembered in the name of one of our trophies - the Elsie Cup. Not only did we know about them, of course, but it transpired that our enquirer was still in touch with one of his relations - Douglas Gordon. Douglas was a school friend of our Editor and the two of them joined Belgrave Harriers as 14 year-olds very many moons ago ... Yes, it is indeed a small world! www.belgraveharriers.com Eric Hall Eric Hall writes the opening story about a walking book bought from New Zealand Norman Read Norman Read the late; 1956 gold medallist Paul Paul in Christchurch, New Zealand Peter Coughlan Peter Coughlan in Christchurch, New Zealand Peter Peter Glenn Hazard Glenn Hazard book seller in Christchurch, NZ; ran London to Brighton road run in the mid seventies Tony Brooks Tony Brooks one time track & field captain; lives in Berryville, Virginia, USA; supplied team photograph on page 9 Tony Tony John Dawson John Dawson Australian; ran for Belgrave as a Junior in the mid-1990s; 1:50 800m and 48.1; now in Tokyo John John Frazer Hazlett Frazer Hazlett former British League squad; now triathlete in Southern California Frazer Frazer Harold Hutchinson Harold Hutchinson competed 1936-38 in sprint hurdles and pole vault Harold Harold Michael Peacock Michael Peacock in South Africa; 49.37 for 400 metres Bob Bridges Bob Bridges coach Nick Molloy Nick Molloy Dotun Akinbogun Dotun Akinbogun Richard David Richard David Richard Mcmillan Richard Mcmillan Joe Panton Joe Panton James Hilston James Hilston John Jeffrey John Jeffrey Mike Small Mike Small Patricia Patricia Alan Mead Alan Mead Ted Pallant Ted Pallant Past President Edwin Gordon Edwin Gordon Past President and one time Mayor of New Malden Elsie Elsie remembered in the Elsie Cup trophy; great aunt of the enquirer Douglas Gordon Douglas Gordon school friend of the Editor; joined Belgrave as a 14 year-old Douglas Douglas London to Brighton road run British League New Zealand Christchurch Essex Berryville, Virginia, USA Shenandoah Valley Belgrave Hall Tokyo Australia Southern California South Africa New Malden

items.s: G.F. Lucas Obituary note for former member George Lucas (born 1914), who joined in 1943 and was 3rd in the club 7 miles cross country championship in 1948. G.F. Lucas Another former member who passed away recently was G.F. Lucas. Born in 1914, George joined the Club during war time in August 1943 and was also a member of Gravesend AC. In 1945 he resigned from the Kent Club and ran in Belgrave colours in various events. Possibly his best year was 1948 when he placed 3rd in our 7 miles Cross Country Championship for the "Blackstaffe Shield" behind Len Herbert and Ted Stimpson. He was second man home in our five and three-quarter mile road race in the same year. G.F. Lucas G.F. items.s: Prolific Marathoner Note on 1960s member Chris Fairfield, now 62 and running for East Cheshire Harriers, who has completed 127 marathons and raised over £70,000 for charity. Prolific Marathoner There must be quite a few members who remember Chris Fairfield, one of our runners back in the '60s. Chris joined us in 1958 but eventually moved to Stalybridge in Cheshire. All this time he has kept up his Belgrave membership although he now, at the age of 62, runs first claim for East Cheshire Harriers. In his time he has clocked up an amazing 127 marathons including 18 Londons and 12 New Yorks and has raised over £70,000 for various charities over the last 15 years. Chris doesn't just stick at marathons either. In February 1998 he trekked to the foothills of Everest for Whizz-Kidz, a charity dedicated to helping provide disabled youngsters with wheelchairs. Last summer Chris competed in the 20 stage Welsh Castles Relay. He was due to run the 18th stage but got stuck in traffic and eventually arrived for his stint 5 minutes late. Nevertheless he set out on the 9.1 mile leg and worked his way through to finish 40th. items.s: Sidetracks . . . Members' news column: Clive Shippen on Foster's running shoes, family arrivals and weddings, Gordon Doubleday's 1930s glider story, injuries, John Powell's new posts, Derek Jones's 25 years with the Women's Southern League, and Belgrave entries for the 1937 Birchfield Harriers Waddilove meeting. Members near and far Sidetracks . . . Clive Shippen writes regarding a couple of items in the last Belgravian: "I could hardly believe that Mark would feature in a '25 Years Ago' item. That really makes me feel old! Regarding 'Footnotes', Reebok only really came to the fore after taking over Foster's of Bolton. Foster's had superseded Law's as the foremost made-to-measure shoemaker in England when Sandy Law declined to compromise his principles by getting involved with what he regarded as the poor quality footwear of Adidas and Puma. Peter Driver was Foster's unofficial representative at one time. Foster did a mail-order service to foot outlines and I well remember giving him my own specification for a thick sandwich sole. This was to off-set the blood blisters I acquired on the soles of my feet during road relays. They worked! But unfortunately they also reduced traction; as I found to my cost in a London-Brighton Relay. Thereafter I wore Foster's ultra-light shoes and accepted the blisters!" It's good to see Maureen and Brian Pritchard attending our functions. Recently Master Thomas Pritchard (born 11/05/1999) was signed up, making him a fourth generation Belgravian. That's got to be a record. Thomas is son of Simon, grandson of Brian and great-grandson of the late Thomas Pritchard who joined 10th June 1924. And talking of new arrivals - congratulations to Jane and Charles Herrington on the safe arrival of baby daughter Hannah May, born on Thursday 12th October and weighing in at 6lbs 10ozs. We missed Charles at the opening Surrey League race at Brockwell Park but sometimes other things just have to take precedence. Gordon Doubleday wrote recently and recalled an incident that occurred to a group of Bels: During the mid 1930s a small group of Belgravians decided to spend the Easter holiday walking on the South Downs, staying at those new-fangled havens the Youth Hostels. They started on the Friday with a slog up to the crest of the Downs. Suddenly, in their path was a glider and walking from it came a suitably clad pilot. He approached our lads and said, "Can you chaps run?" He wanted some people to grab the ropes attached to his machine and run, dragging the glider until airborne. Our lads duly complied and, at a signal from the pilot, sprinted along the springy downland turf. He was soon airborne and our lads continued their walk westwards towards Lewes. They paused to take a look skywards. The glider was now well aloft and the pilot gave them a wave of thanks. Could those chaps run? Like Hell they could - and did! And what of the antics of today's lads. With our running Captain Roger Alsop due to marry Helen Maskrey, our Skipper decided to hold his stag celebrations over the weekend of the Surrey Road Relay which became the first event in the most confusing and violently contested multi-event competition that the participants had ever entered into. Apart from the normal over-indulgences, Go Kart racing resulted in a most spectacular crash involving Bruce Barton and his Cross Country Team Manager (poor Bruce was unable to run for weeks) while the exploits on the golf course saw a Belgravian on an adjacent fairway struck on the rump by a Belgrave impelled ball while all around rolled about helpless with laughter. Charlie Dickinson was victor ludorum while Roger received the contents of a bucket of cold water at the last watering hole of the day. Helen and Roger were duly wed on October 6th at the Registry Office in Morden with the reception held at a recently decorated and immaculate Hall in Denmark Rd., SW19. Needless to say many Belgravians were there to wish them well. Congratulations to Steve Clarke who has married Kerrie. Kerrie is a Shaftesbury Barnet Harrier but we won't hold that against her. The Clarkes honeymooned in Sydney and had planned things well, taking in Steve Redgrave's gold medal winning effort in the rowing and plenty of Belgrave action in the main Stadium. On one of the Manly ferries across the harbour a fellow traveller commented on Steve's Belgrave track top: "I used to compete for Belgrave Harriers." It turned out to be Graham Seatter who sends his regards to all who remember him. Our Hon. Treasurer Dave McMillan and Paula Lively were wed in the Oxfordshire village of Marston on 24th June. Bruce Barton and Amanda married in Shepperton on 15th July and honeymooned in the USA and the Bahamas, while Nikki Haines, key member of our medal winning London Marathon squad last Spring, married Graeme Neal in Alderney on 27th December. George Flanagan married Anne. Our very best wishes go to all of them. Tony Stone recently had a fall while running on the Common, resulting in a broken bone in his foot and a four day spell in hospital. He is now hobbling about on crutches but it didn't stop him from getting up to Belgrave Hall on the day of our home men's Surrey League race. He now has a plate in his foot but no doubt we'll see him back jogging before too long. Also in the wars a little while back was Dennis Jones. At Wimbledon Station while heading for the Hall he was badly bitten on the hand by a dog. While medical assistance was called for Dennis was quite adamant: "It wasn't the dog's fault. I startled it". We are sorry to report that our old comrade Dave McMullen is now incapacitated and in a nursing home. For those of his club-mates who would like to write to Dave, or maybe call in and see him, the address is [address withheld]. John Powell is not one to stay idle. Having retired as Team Manager of our most successful ever Junior T&F team he has taken on posts as Secretary to the AAA of England (T&F) and British and English Junior Indoor Team Manager. He continues to provided administrative backup to our Young Athletes' Section and is now putting the finishing touches to our Child Protection Policy. And of course he continues to coach some of the best young sprinters in the country. Derek Jones celebrates 25 years of association with our Women's Southern League this summer. During that time he has been Women's Secretary, Team Manager, Coach, Field Event Judge and is currently the Division Three Administrator. Well done Derek. There is plenty of talent in the Lambert family. Not only have the Lambert boys featured in all of our young athletes' teams with father Jon as Team Manager, but there is artistic talent as well. 18 year-old Alex has designed an eye-catching poster and brochure which is being used in schools across South London in our 2001 recruitment drive. Visiting Lichfield en route to the National 6 stage relay one of our avid collectors of athletic memorabilia found a secondhand bookshop and bought a programme for the Birchfield Harriers Diamond Jubilee meeting, incorporating the Waddilove meeting, dated 24 July 1937. Belgrave entries for that meeting included E Gray (100 yds) T D Wiley (100 yds) reserves F W Pritchard and S C Botwright. 440 yds D G Michael, H E Pack, reserves T H Scrimshaw & A A Bird. 880 yds L W Herbert, A A Bird reserves T H Scrimshaw, W E Lucas, F H C White. 2 Mile Scratch team L J Cohen, J Parker, A W Penny, C T Carter, D Patience, J Ginty, E S Stimpson, H W Shields. 1 Mile Relay inter Club (880+440+220+220): E Gray, T D Wiley, S C Botwright, F W Pritchard, H E Pack, R G Michael, T H Scrimshaw, A A Bird, L W Herbert, F H C White, F R Webb, W E Lucas. According to the Belgravian (August 1937) "we sent a team to Birmingham to compete in the Waddilove Trophy track competition for the first time. Birchfield Harriers have been anxious for years that we should participate, and at our first attempt we were glad to become joint holders, with the London A C of the handsome trophy. We were successful in winning the Two Mile team race through the efforts of A W Penny, L J Cohen and E S Stimpson; and took second place in the Relay (won by Birchfield), our team being A A Bird, R G Michael, S C Botwright and E Gray. In addition Bird ran wonderfully well to finish second to J V Powell, beaten by a yard and a half in 1 min. 57 3/5 seconds. E Gray was placed third in the 100 yds. Final scores were Belgrave H and L A C 12 points each; Birchfield H., 10 pts; the holders, Achilles, scoring 1 point only. All our runners did very well, and we returned feeling well satisfied with or first visit to Perry Bar."
