items.s: NATIONAL 12-STAGE ROAD RELAY: Out of the chaos - bronze medals Stage-by-stage report of Belgrave's bronze medals in the ERRA Men's 12-Stage Road Relay at Sutton Park on 8 April 2006, after entry mix-ups kept Paul Freary out of the team. ERRA Men's 12-Stage Road Relay, Sutton Park, Sutton Coldfield, 8 April 2006. This was no occasion for the faint of heart. An Achilles tendon injury took out long stager Hassan Raidi three days before the race but we were already concealing the fact that David Anderson had been unable to run at all since the previous Friday due to a calf muscle problem. We hoped against hope that he would recover in time and in the event, David ruled himself ok with two days to go. We breathed again as, already missing the talents of Spencer Barden, Kevin Nash and Mark Miles, we were desperately short of long stage backup. In spite of all of this, an undoubtedly good and excitingly young team hoped to secure another National win. Then, only half an hour before the start, we were hit by the shock that our planned first stage runner was not going to be allowed to run. Unaccountably it seemed that Paul Freary's name had been left off of the list of 72 names from which our A and B teams could be selected. There is no doubt that it was our own mistake and the Team Manager was absolutely “gutted” by his oversight. An appeal to the Race Referee met with a stone wall response. “You cannot run him - if you do then you will be disqualified.” While struggling to cope with this the TM then found that Richard Ward's name was also not on the declaration list. This seemed unbelievable - but reference to a photocopy of our entry showed that Richard HAD been entered. Another audience with the Referee was needed: “Ok, if you can prove that you did enter him then he can take part.” Our response: “But surely you can now see how a minor administrative error can be made by either party. Surely an athlete should not be penalised for such an oversight.” Sadly, there was no softening of attitude. It seemed that the official line was to be more accommodating with their own mistake than with ours. Chaos ensued as the team order was hastily changed to bring in a reserve, and then changed again to avoid running him when it was suggested that an appeal against the Referee's decision might be worth pursuing. A couple of long stages and five short stages were brought forward to give breathing space during which time we hoped the judgment could be changed. In the end it was not to be and, in hindsight, it was probably the right decision. Imagine the slating we would get if allowed to medal - or perhaps win - with an un-entered runner. The day was as windy as we can ever remember at Sutton Park, becoming very cold and finishing with a hail storm and freezing rain. Stage 1 Karl O'Connell, the man due to start off the Bs was at first drafted in to take Paul Freary's place but the need not to bring in a reserve until we knew the decision had gone against us changed that plan, and with a minimum warm-up, A-team member Tim Watson came forward a leg. He'd arrived at the hotel in the small hours of the morning having finished work at 10pm in Dartmouth, Devon! Tough these Marines - and he was fired up too, running well and only ten seconds off the lead as the pack returned from the far end of the park. Sale H Manchester were rumoured to be at full strength and looking for the win, and through Stuart Stokes they made an early bid to complete the initial stage 12 seconds clear. Tim suffered from stitch on the last section of the lap, probably brought on by the upset in his eating schedule through coming on early, and he lost 30 seconds in the final mile or so. But 12th was a good start and all our expected rivals were close by, with the exception of the Beagles - back in 25th. 1 S Stokes (Sale) 26:21; 2 M Lole (Coventry G) 26:33 3 M Scaife (Morpeth) 26:35; 4 B Raeside (Notts) 26:41; 5 M Hilton (Leeds) 26:41; 6 D Norman (Altrincham) 26:42; 12 T Watson 27:03; 61 J Fairbourn 'B' 30:34. Stage 2 On his favourite second stage, Richard Ward was on song, his sub-15 bringing us up five places as he was chased all the way by Aldershot's Chris Bolt. Ex-Belgravian Rick Hayman kept Sale's colours near the front while back down the field Karl O'Connell, who by this time had worn more race numbers than contained in the Sutton Coldfield telephone directory, thanks to the team switches, had a great run for the Bs, moving past a dozen rivals. 1 Coventry (+1) 41:18; 2 Morpeth (+1) 41:24; 3 Sale HM (-2) 41:26; 4 Derby (+4) 41:32; 5 Leeds C (0) 41:38; 6 Sunderland (+5) 41:49; 7 Belgrave 'A' (+5) 41:59; 49 Belgrave 'B' (+12) 46:08. Fastest: 1 J Mellor (Liverpool) 14:33; 2 R Weir (Derby) and B Jones (Coventry) 14:45; 9 R Ward 14:56; ... K O'Connell 'B' 15:34. Stage 3 We were playing a stronger hand than bargained for at this stage of the race and Simon Jones pushed things along even more, pulling back two more places and keeping very good company with the likes of Andy Vernon (Aldershot) and Rob Birchall (Notts). National cross country champions Leeds City were now making the pace and were race favourites in the eyes of many but Bob Smith's Beagles were coming back - now in 11th. If the Bels felt that bad luck had dogged them at all on this day, consider the sorry state of affairs for Bedford & County. Having lost a handful of runners before the race, a thief visited their tent and stole treasured items belonging to one of their number and as a result he lost the will to race. He was replaced by a reserve - who then badly pulled a calf muscle but somehow kept going to the end of the stage to hand over in 63rd and last place. It was now obvious that the blustery conditions were having a huge effect. Not one long stage runner had gone below 26 minutes at this point. 1 Leeds C (+4) 1:07:54; 2 Coventry G (-1) 1:08:58; 3 Morpeth (-1) 1:09:04; 4 Altrincham (+5) 1:09:06; 5 Belgrave (+2) 1:09:08; 6 Aldershot F&D (+2) 1:09:10; 51 Belgrave 'B' (-2) 30:51. Stage 4 Last man into the SEAA team at Milton Keynes, Pete Willis was raided from the Bs here at Sutton Park to plug the gap caused by the removal of Paul Freary from the line-up. Obviously we were expecting to go back here as Pete was dropped into a bubbling cauldron but, just as two weeks earlier, he raised his game accordingly. Only three positions were lost by the Belgravian and two of these were due to scorchers from Jackson (Sale) and Hepples (Newham &EB). Pete had done an absolutely brilliant job and the success of the Tom Osment coached squad was added to by eighteen year-old Joe van der Toorn who took the Bs up six places. 1 Leeds C (0) 1:23:04; 2 Sale HM (+5) 1:23:36; 3 Morpeth (0) 1:23:53; 4 Aldershot F&D (+2) 1:24:01; 5 Newham &EB (+6) 1:24:07; 6 Coventry G (-4) 1:24:33; 8 Belgrave (-3) 1:24:42; 45 Belgrave 'B' (+6) 1:32:48. Fastest: 1 S Hepples (Newham &EB) 14:18; 2 E Jackson (Sale HM) 14:23; 3 J Mays (Kent) 14:30; ... P Willis 15:34; J van der Toorn 15:49. Stage 5 At this point the 'B' team became disqualifiable as Paul Freary set out under the name of Stephen Zealey, taking them up 11 places. But eight minutes up the road Will Cockerell had played his Captain's role well, moving up to a long stage to let in the short stage reserve Pete Willis, and running several seconds faster than his first stage effort of last year, run in more benign conditions. Well done Will! Our problems had probably cost us 50 seconds - maybe a minute. We were 2 minutes 19 seconds behind the leaders - still Leeds - but more ominously 1:17 down on the Beagles; we had a great line-up to come but, frankly, so did they. 1 Leeds C (0) 1:50:15; 2 Newham &EB (+3) 1:51:07; 3 Altrincham (+7) 1:51:13; 4 Notts (+5) 1:51:18; 5 Sale HM (-3) 1:51:26; 6 Bristol &W (+1) 1:51:37; 9 Belgrave (-1) 1:52:34; 34 Belgrave 'B' (+11) 2:00:08. Stage 6 The wind was now atrocious; but as a club tent opposite our own was ripped from the ground and deposited in the branches of an obliging tree, Darren Gauson toured the short stage in our first of only two fastest stages of the day. By now aware of what the East London club had to come, most supporters had switched to backing the Beagles for the win (AW correspondent Martin Duff still persisted with the thought that it would be Leeds) but we pulled back half a minute on both of them thanks to Darren. All was not yet lost. 1 Leeds C (0) 2:05:32; 2 Sale HM (+3) 2:06:20; 3 Newham &EB (-1) 2:06:24; 4 Bristol &W (+2) 2:06:46; 5 Notts (-1) 2:07:09; 6 Aldershot F&D (+2) 2:07:11; 7 Belgrave (+2) 2:07:23; 33 Belgrave 'B' (+1) 2:16:24. Fastest: 1 D Gauson (Belgrave) 14:49; 2 J Bailey (Sale HM) 14:54; 3 S Ablitt (Aldershot F&D) 14:55; ... J Webb ('B') 16:16. Stage 7 It was Stephen Sharp's first attempt at a long stage and one would have liked to have thought that the extra distance to be covered by our speedster might give us the chance to recover some ground. Not so! Mark Warmby of the Beagles took nearly half a minute out of Leeds but he in turn was being chased down by Bristol's Rob Whalley. Still in 7th, it was going to be an almighty battle for the Bels to reach the medals. 1 Leeds C (0) 2:32:09; 2 Newham &EB (+1) 2:32:34; 3 Bristol &W (+1) 2:32:50; 4 Sale HM (-2) 2:33:02; 5 Altrincham (+3) 2:33:46; 6 Aldershot F&D (0) 2:33:52; 7 Belgrave (0) 2:34:08; 34 Belgrave 'B' (-1) 2:46:44. Fastest: 1 R Whalley (Bristol &W) 26:04; 2 M Warmby (Newham &EB) 26:10; 3 A Norman (Altrincham) 26:15; 8 S Sharp 26:45 ... M Humphrey 30:20. Stage 8 Long time leaders Leeds were under severe pressure now. Chris Thompson ran the fastest time of the day to bring Aldershot up into the frame for the first time but also pulling back ground, if only one place, Chris Moss ran our fastest short stage so far. The final top six had now been established and all of them went through the take-over zone in less than one minute - but which would be the three to gain the medals? 1 Leeds C (0) 2:47:38; 2 Newham &EB (0) 2:47:41; 3 Aldershot F&D (+3) 2:47:54; 4 Bristol &W (-1) 2:48:08; 5 Sale HM (-1) 2:48:12; 6 Belgrave (+1) 2:48:35; 33 Belgrave 'B' (+1) 3:04:39. Fastest: C Thompson (Aldershot F&D 14:02; 2 C Moss (Belgrave) 14:27; 3 D Robinson (Stroud &D) 14:31; ... R Poulter ('B') 17:55. Stage 9 “Oh Yes!” shouted Mo Farah, unable to contain his exhilaration when the announcer indicated that the incoming runner from Newham & Essex Beagles was only 3 seconds down on the leaders. And his excitement was not in vain, for this was where the gold medals were decided. Also going into action, for the Bels, was Phil Wicks. Just 22 years of age and with only four years of running on the clock, Phil's 26:35 was superb - and again, in spite of the conditions, nearly half a minute faster than the previous year. Mo's was far and away the day's fastest long stage and the Beagles went into the last quarter of the race with over one and a half minutes to spare over Sale, who, together with Leeds, were now within striking distance of both Aldershot and Belgrave. An interesting thought at this point: but for our team entry problem, Mossy might have given Phil the task of setting out alongside Mo Farah at the start of this stage! 1 Newham &EB (+1) 3:13:08; 2 Sale HM (+3) 3:14:41; 3 Leeds C (-2) 3:14:51; 4 Aldershot F&D (-1) 3:14:54; 5 Belgrave (+1) 3:15:10; 6 Bristol &W (-2) 3:15:44; 49 Belgrave 'B' (-16) 3:42:07. Fastest: 1 M Farah (Newham &EB) 25:27; 2 G Cornish (Sale HM) 26:29; 3 P Wicks (Belgrave) 26:35; ... H Corbett M45 ('B') 37:28. Stage 10 By now there was sleet and hail in the air. Kris Gauson may be 18 but he has some extraordinary racing times behind him, having in his two years of membership already relieved John Gladwin of his Youth club records for 800m and 1500m. His 15:15 cemented our position in the top four and now made medals a strong possibility. Newham's Stuart Major has had a patch of poor health and while not in the best of form, he was as solid as a rock and with Dave Mitchinson to come, nobody was going to get back to the Beagles. A final brush with officialdom came when we offered an additional and final runner to the 'B' team's complement - D. Anderson. “Have you cleared this with the Referee?” came the retort when the name was declared. (A Belgravian of very similar name had just finished the 11th stage for the As.) “No. And we don't intend to! This is Don Anderson.” 1 Newham &EB (0) 3:28:20; 2 Sale HM (0) 3:29:39; 3 Leeds C (0) 3:30:00; 4 Belgrave (+1) 3:30:25; 5 Aldershot F&D (-1) 3:30:52; 6 Bristol &W (0) 3:31:09; 50 Belgrave 'B' (-1) 4:01:24. Fastest: 1 M Bond (Sale HM) 14:58; 2 A Osbourne (Leeds C) 15:09; 3 S Major (Newham &EB) 15:12; 4 K Gauson (Belgrave) 15:15; ... Don Anderson ('B') 19:17. Stage 11 The gap to Leeds and bronze was 25 seconds; the gap to Sale and silver was a further 21 seconds. Anything could happen here. Well, something did happen; yet another twist in an extraordinary day. David Anderson set out looking pumped up but when spotted by our supporters at the top of the hill they noted the lack of fluency in his running. David was in trouble. That calf muscle had almost immediately tightened and in trying to isolate the muscle and restrict its use to avoid further damage and pain, the hamstring and gluteal muscles also tightened. We've no doubt that pulling out was not an option in his mind - and somehow, David held the gap to Leeds and clocked equal fourth fastest on the stage. An heroic run - but now our man faces yet more rehabilitation before getting back to his athletic career. 1 Newham &EB (0) 3:55:08; 2 Sale HM (0) 3:56:31; 3 Leeds C (0) 3:57:24; 4 Belgrave (0) 3:57:49; 5 Bristol &W (+1) 3:58:25; 6 Aldershot F&D (-1) 3:58:38. Fastest: 1 D Mitchison (Newham &EB 26:48; 2 D Augustus (Sale HM) 26:52; 3 C Nicholson (Bristol &W) 27:16; =4 D Anderson (Belgrave) 27:24. Stage 12 It had always been felt that the race for first place could be tight over the final stage. In fact it didn't turn out that way - but, for the first time in his road relay career at Sutton Park, Jonathan Blackledge set out in full cry with a runner in sight. One had to feel sorry for the Leeds City team. They'd led from stages 3 to 8 and then occupied third place for stages 9 to 11, only to have one the country's most voracious young runners unleashed on their tail, eager to feed on the scraps left over by the Beagles. Jonathan brought us into the bronze medal position and such was his pace that the smell of Sale blood was in his nostrils at the race end. He was fastest on his stage and third fastest of the day in spite of the worsening conditions; and but for those conditions we may have been close to only our third ever sub-14 clocking by a Belgravian. Don't know about you - but this writer felt pretty shattered by the end of all this, until the realisation dawned: this young team had responded tremendously to the setbacks ... they have years of relay racing ahead of them in which some really exciting events should unfold ... our medal streak has extended to six years ... a young man had come along not dreaming that by the end of the day he'd be going home with a National medal ... we'd all received a jolt to remind ourselves what a tough job it is to get everything in winning order ... and we are even more hardened and determined to face the road battles ahead in Sutton Park. 1 Newham &EB (0) 4:10:08; 2 Sale HM (0) 4:11:39; 3 Belgrave (+1) 4:12:09; 4 Leeds C (-1) 4:12:31; 5 Bristol &W (0) 4:13:04; 6 Aldershot F&D (0) 4:13:55; 66 teams started, 62 teams finished. items.s: From The Belgravian: 75 Years Ago – 1931 Extracts from a 1931 Belgravian report of the London to Brighton Relay of 11 April 1931, in which Belgrave placed fifth. 75 Years Ago – 1931 April 11th, 1931 – the day appointed for the London to Brighton Relay – now one of the most popular sporting events in the South – proved to be a very fine day with glorious sunshine … Our 'bus arrived at Westminster … and was soon transformed into a combined dressing room and moving grandstand. Posters in Club colours invoked “Up the Bels,” and the claret and gold rosettes, ties and scarves (not forgetting the beret of our Running Hon. Secretary's wife!) gave our 'bus a very colourful appearance. Several bells also made their presence known, and if it had been possible to transform the energy used by the ringers into running power, we should have been in Brighton before the other teams reached Crawley! Our 'bus left Westminster … and we made for Clapham Common, where our first man Jack Flower would hand on to Alfred Kench. … we had made a very good start for Jack was lying fourth … and was only four seconds outside last year's record for this stretch … Kench carried on and quickly found that he was running in the highest class … his first appearance for the Club in an important race took the form of an “ordeal by fire” … he lost places to men … of far greater experience , but none surpassed him for plucky running. … He arrived at Mitcham still fighting gallantly and almost “all-in” in tenth position, but well within striking distance of those in front, now led by Tipton H. Duffett now ran for us, and … our man picked up three opponents but had to sacrifice two positions and so handed over ninth … Birchfield H had now taken the lead and … were not to be headed again. Our best men were still to run and those in front were spread out at intervals of twenty or thirty yards. This looked like helping Arthur Allum to smash the record for the fourth stage, and to bring us up to second or third … but … he had covered 2½ miles and picked up four positions when his ankle gave way, and from this point it was a case of gritting teeth and struggling on in pain … we were now seventh … he was unable to put his foot to the ground after finishing … and later was prescribed a month's rest. Despite this accident, Allum had accomplished a very fast time compared with other runners over the stretch, and but for this unfortunate occurrence we should have been on the heels of the leaders. Sid Warboys … pegged back Hallamshire and Surrey AC and handed over fifth. Joe Flower carried on the good work, overhauling Highgate and Tipton and bringing us up to third. Bert Footer ran next and although he ran faster than any other Belgrave man has done in the past over this stretch, he was forced to surrender places to Tipton H. and Surrey AC. C. Mains, a young man of twenty, running his first race for us … did very well over what is, perhaps, the most difficult stage of the lot … the gradual ascent of the South Downs, culminating in the climb of Dale Hill. Only once has a Belgrave man beaten Mains' time, and … we gained 19 seconds upon Tipton Harriers. C.T. Carter, one of our first year runners, was entrusted with the last stage … there was little to worry about … we placed fifth, a creditable performance. Next year we may well be fighting out the lead … Some words of praise are due to our reserves, who continued to train conscientiously up to the day of the race in order to give of their best if called upon. This is just another little indication of the team spirit which is carrying us forward. … 1 Birchfield H 4:48:58; 2 South London H 4:49:31; 3 Surrey AC 4:49:41; 4 Tipton H 4:51:15; 5 Belgrave H 4:53:27; 6 Hallamshire H 4:54:13. items.s: Skipper's Corner The club captain's column reflecting on the SEAA and National 12-Stage relays of 2006, past Belgrave relay teams and the entry mix-up at Sutton Park. March 28, 2006 - This is sport - if there were no problems it would be too easy Sunday [SEAA 12-Stage] was a day for reflection in many ways. The chaps and the dames who run Belgrave are forever looking ahead, in their attempts to keep the club in sound health, but to do this it often helpful to look to the past, where the fingerprints to the future lie. What were we doing 15 years ago – and 10 – and 5? Were we making mistakes - have we put them right? I was given a fine window into the past by travelling to the race with Alan's team letter and directions for not this year (that'd be way too organized), but from that of 2000. It is clear that he wrote his tub-thumping letter to the runners that year sensing that we were finally a club on the up, after years of false dawns and mediocrity. Our success on the track had arrived in the 90s, and now perhaps, we could strike it big on the road. In his Milton Keynes letter of 2000, Alan speaks of how the team was looking 'rock solid', and that we had a real chance of winning. Rock solid turned into mass capitulation, as, after he wrote the letter, half a dozen runners bowed out with various excuses. The runner for leg 11 was hauled out of the B's the night before, and slung into the A's despite having only placed 235/253 the year before. Photos from the 2000 race show him sporting a spectacular comb-over, as he slugged it out with Shaftesbury's Nick Francis, a mere four-and-a-half minutes separating their 'pb's'. We ended up with a hard-fought bronze that day, and the leg 11 runner is the only survivor from the 2000 A-team to appear in the 2006 edition, minus sadly the comb-over. It was bronze again the following year as only two relics survive (Me and Wardy – if you can call a 23-year-old a relic!) Surely no-one survives from the silver medal team of 1999 … but one does – even if he did memorably break the two cardinal rules of relay-running: don't get lost, and don't walk. Dear old Hassan did both and was promptly sent to the naughty chair for a few seasons. But his return to the fold in 2003 has seen him become a highly valued member, striking National gold in all sorts of events: 10k, half-marathon, cross-country. Four master-blasters What our teams lacked in those pre-2002 days were three elusive things: youth – average age's veered the wrong side of 30; solidity – teams would bear little resemblance to the ones on the team sheet; and the 'X-factor': a lack of runners with that something 'a bit special' – who could turn a race on its head. We don't have an X-factor runner now, either. As it happens, we've got four. In SS, DA, Wicksy and Jon, we have four master-blasters who form the foundation upon which our teams are built, with an average age of just 25. Long may they continue. Was Sunday an anti-climax because of our dominance? I don't think so! Not when you think of our support staff, who were there: The Halls, the Meads, Gordon, Don, Bill, Rex and the President, you can tot up nearly 400 years of dedicated Belgrave service between them. Seeing our team perform as such a magnificent, coherent unit owes a lot to their vision, belief, and determination. In the neighbouring tent we enjoyed Gerry North's company – the ultimate X-factor man. April 10, 2006 - I've seen it all before Well, I think my 146th race for a Belgrave team [National 12-Stage] was the one in which I felt the widest range of emotions… And one thing I do know – I've seen it all before. Do you recognize these words from the pen of the team manager?: “It was very quiet inside the Belgrave tent for a while. The shock of having the prize snatched away was stunning. But this group of runners is much more than a team. There is a feeling for each other that rival clubs do not see when they look at Belgrave from the outside. Spencer Barden was soon upbeat: 'Don't worry. Next year we'll do it.' ” The words come from ARM's report of the epic National 12 of 2001 – of which 'relic Wardy' survives. [Wardy said that day he'd fancy 20 runs at this great event… Well - he's six for six. Surely he can't be serious!] Was Spen deluded with his optimistic chirrup? Er, not really, when you consider we won the next year by 6-and-a-half minutes, and then in 2003 as well. We've been through this before boys, and our average age has markedly dropped as well (27 years and four months in 2001, 25 years and one month in 2006). And both Tim and I like to think of ourselves as a young 32! Far more good has come out of this race than bad: our young lions have been given a healthy dose reality – success in events like this don't come easy, first you must pay your dues. The “National 12” has its credibility and charisma back, as it attracted masses of good runners and six fine squads. Newham were more than good value for their win – that was a fantastic team – congratulations. Here are my top five reflections on the day: 1) Alan and I kneeling by the recorders hut like two earnest schoolboys trying to crack a riddle on a treasure hunt. There were less than two minutes to the gun and we were desperately trying to reselect our team and construct a running order. “What letter comes after E in the alphabet?” “H” “Are you sure?” “Yep, no, maybe G.” “Ok cool.” “Put in Willis there…no O'Connell…no Willis…no O'Connell…” [They ended up firing identical times!] “Put Blackledge on 8,” I'd gabble. “No way man – he doesn't move.” “Put me on 11,” I'd suggest. “But you're going short!” “Yes, yes, but I might be going long.” “Put Gauson on 4.” “Which one?” “The tall one with the curly reddish hair.” “Darren!?” “No! Kris.” “Can't, he's just eaten…” And on and on it went. I admit it, both of our fried little minds were in meltdown. 2) The look on my chum and training partner Stuart Major's face at prize-giving. Stui has trained week in, week out for a day like this since the mid-to-late 1980s. He's run 17 of the last 18 National cross champs and has won scores of races. Nobody deserves his medal more. Having barely run a session in five weeks due to a virus, he ran his stage on memory. “I've never seen one of these before!” he said, as he gazed at his nugget of gold. Marvellous. 3) Mo Farah's stage. The look of heartbreak on his face as he just failed to catch Spen at the National 6 in '01 is embedded in my memory palace. He just stood there afterwards, completely drained, despairing and shell-shocked. I also recall an unfit Mo fighting like a tiger at the Southern 6 in '02 – he was on the verge of collapse that day too – but slow down? Never! His triumphant tour on Saturday was five long years in the making. “Looks like he's out for a training spin,” said the spectators on the first rise.” “Yep, I don't think he's taking today too seriously,” said another. “He's not even running in a straight line…” I desperately wanted to believe these scraps from the peanut gallery – but deep down I knew we were dead. 4) The Blackledge-Roscoe duel on stage 12 was run between two hugely consistent and dedicated runners. Martin Roscoe has been in the scoring six for Leeds in every single one of the last nine National cross-champs, during which time they've been a cut above everyone else. Tremendously tough, he enjoys legendary status in Northern club athletics. Over 7 miles of Parly Hill bog, I think I know who I'd back… but over the macadam of Sutton Park, Jon's lithe stride was just too fluent – his nerve, as ever, ice cool. 5) A tie for the Bel man-of-the-match between DA's excruciating turn, and Paul's selfless and cheerful demeanour at being given the hammer blow news. If one has to take around 5,000 strides on a long stage, Danders must have died 2,500 times on his bad leg. And does Paul merely cruise round for the B's? No! he runs at 95% and hoists them a dozen or so places up the field… Belgrave couldn't wish for two finer elder statesmen in their squad. A solid season So mission 5-6 is over and if we look at my dispatch from September 7, it goes down as a solid season – three titles. But the club is in even better shape than when we set out seven months ago, and it won't be easy to wait until September to do it all over again. Meanwhile, have a great summer everyone, and thanks for the memories. items.sum: Report of Phil Wicks winning the Maidenhead 10 miles for the third consecutive year in 48:34, with Belgrave first team.
items.s: Wicks the Wizard! Report of Phil Wicks winning the Maidenhead 10 miles for the third consecutive year in 48:34, with Belgrave first team. A fabulous breakthrough came from Phil Wicks, winning the Maidenhead 10 miles for the third consecutive year - in a time of 48:34. He went through 5 miles in 24:07 - a personal best - 6m in 28:55 and 7m in 33:49. A 15:10 was needed for the last three miles to enable him to crack 49 minutes (his pre-race target had been to break 50) and he turned on a magnificent 14:44. Mike Trees was 5th (1st Veteran – and good to see him running again after a severe dental operation) in 54:55, Joachim Wolf 7th in 55:21 – and the Bels were first team. items.sum: Notice that long-time member Roger Alsop, former Running Captain and Club Secretary, has resigned after moving to Edinburgh.
items.s: Roger and out Notice that long-time member Roger Alsop, former Running Captain and Club Secretary, has resigned after moving to Edinburgh. Roger Alsop, a long time Belgravian, turned out for Herne Hill Harriers in the SEAA 12-stage and clocked a short stage time which would still have got him into our A team. Roger's switch of clubs was triggered by his desire to get into veteran team competition but he retained second-claim membership of the Bels. However, moving home to Edinburgh has caused him to reconsider and he has now resigned. So, 16 years of membership, during which time he became our Running Captain and Club Secretary, comes to an end. We thank you Roger for all you have done and wish you well. Roger Alsop Roger Alsop 16 years a member; former Running Captain and Club Secretary; resigned 2006 Roger Roger SEAA 12-Stage Road Relay Edinburgh Herne Hill Harriers

items.sum: Note that Marty Dent, writing from Australia after the Commonwealth Games steeplechase, congratulated the club and was selected for the World Cross in Fukuoka.
items.s: Marty sends congrats Note that Marty Dent, writing from Australia after the Commonwealth Games steeplechase, congratulated the club and was selected for the World Cross in Fukuoka. Marty Dent, fresh from his great run in the Commonwealth Games steeplechase, writes from Australia and sends congratulations on a fifth consecutive SEAA 12-Stage win. Marty, who tells us that he regularly checks the Belgrave website for news, has been selected to compete in both the short and long course cross country events at the World Cross in Fukuoka, Japan this weekend. He also tells us that he may be over this summer for some races in Europe and would love to slot in a few warm-up races for the Bels. items.sum: Bill Laws's report and results from British Athletics League Premiership Division Match One at Barnet Copthall on 6 May 2006, which a young Belgrave team won on the relays.
items.s: British Athletics League Bill Laws's report and results from British Athletics League Premiership Division Match One at Barnet Copthall on 6 May 2006, which a young Belgrave team won on the relays. Premiership Division, Match One, Barnet Copthall Stadium, 6 May 2006. Young squad fights back for the win The first match of the season is when management act more like travel agents than team leaders, writes Bill Laws. Their first task is to check who is still abroad, when will they be returning, and then to approach the delicate task of when they plan to compete. A number of our team valiantly answered the call with the record going to James Ellington who flew in to the UK at 2.00am match day and still managed to make a valuable contribution to both relays. As the day turned out Belgrave spirits moved in the opposite direction to the weather, which started bright and sunny but turned gloomy and ended with torrential rain. Gloom had already descended on the Belgrave supporters after the first few events which suffered from below par performances: a “no height” in the pole vault and a “no distance” in the hammer, while Commonwealth games returnees, Mick Jones and Matt Douglas, suffered a drop in performance and paid the price. Similarly the discus performances were below par and worryingly Scot Thompson was referred for a medical assessment on what seemed to be a displaced neck vertebrae. A ray of hope from Ryan Ryan Dinham, back after a year of injury, produced the first ray of hope by winning the B 400H in a time faster than the A winner. To reward him for this magnificent effort the team managers allowed him to run the B 800m 30 minutes later and his single point could well have proved important as by this time the team score was about 50 points below planned and the Bels were languishing in 5th spot. But then … the sun was still shining. To be fair to Ryan - his single point would doubtless have been more had he not tightened a hamstring just when considering a move up the field at 600m. The A race had seen Joe van der Toorn, suffering from a cold, boldly step up from the B after a late withdrawal caught us on the hop. It all started to turn round And then, as the clouds rolled in, it all started to turn around. A second place in the A long jump (Adrian Phillips) backed by a win in the B (Richard Danso) was followed by good points in the A 100 where we saw the welcome return of Darren Chin (who lost last season through injury) backed up in the B 100 by Phillips Idowu (honing his speed). The ever reliable Will Cockerell produced one point more than anticipated in the steeplechase and then came our only maximum point event of the day as William Sharman won the A 110H in deteriorating conditions and Dom Girdler did likewise in the B race. William had previously won the non scoring 100 in a time faster than the B 100 winner and continues to confound and amaze the team managers. Our youngest pairing The shot saw our youngest pairing square up to some elder statesmen and they acquitted themselves with distinction. Chris Gearing was a clear second to Woodford’s Emeka Udechuku in the A competition while yet another returnee from injury, Mark Allen, produced a pb to win the B shot. Then followed two hours of sublime track competition as the Premiership match events alternated with the Division 1 match which was being held in conjunction. In the A 400 Set Osho continued to show improvement in a season which has only just started for him, while decathlete Louis Evling-Jones was another one who missed last season through injury but ran the field down on the home straight to snatch a fine second spot in the B 400. The skies opened At about 3pm the skies opened to chill and soak the 1500m men. Eighteen year-old Kris Gauson was looking for a fast time after finishing third in the previous week’s BUSA’s and he was not disappointed as a high class field ignored the conditions and followed in the wake of Essex Beagle Mark Warmby who looked determined to lead from gun to tape. Kris gradually worked through the field and with 200m to go sprinted after the leader whom he just failed to catch while the Valley’s Ben Tickner sneaked silver in a last gasp lunge for the line. Kris was rewarded with a big pb and is getting himself a reputation. And who should be just a few paces behind but Richard Ward who not only won the B 1500 but showed that he too is beginning to get back some of the old sparkle. And then two second places in the 200 with A runner Harry Aikines-Aryeetey finding the conditions very different from his recent training camp in the USA. More good points came from Darren Chin in the B 200. He is clearly not race fit but getting through this without injury is a key step on his road to recovery. Best BAL middle distance race in ten years And then to the 5000m which many of those present thought was the best middle distance BAL race in depth they had seen over the last 10 years. With 8 runners finishing in under 14 min 15 secs in appalling conditions the athletes owed it to Phil Wicks who hit the front early and relentlessly ground out a fast pace for the next eight laps only to find the big guns were still there. Andy Coleman, of Enfield, jumped with 600 to go and was followed by an attentive Newham man in the form of Steve Hepples. Stephen Sharp (another who had returned recently from warm weather training in Portugal) sprinted to cover and passed Hepples but failed to catch Coleman. Phil stuck to his guns and both he and Stephen were rewarded with big pb’s. More excellent scores and Belgrave were suddenly leading by 19 points. In the field we welcomed back Seni Majekodunmi. He, and late stand in Darragh O’Farrell (who had broken a leg in a decathlon pole vault in Ireland during the winter), kept the score ticking along before the high jump result knocked us back again. The late withdrawal of our A string saw the ubiquitous William Sharman promoted and despite not having jumped since last year he mixed it with the best in still atrocious conditions to clear 2m. Dalton Grant only beat him on count back. Our B man Louis Evling-Jones was still running his B 400 as the high jump started due to a 30 minute delay in the track program. By the time he had recovered sufficiently to consider any vertical movement the bar was at 1.95. Too high for him to enter the competition. So, 6 points from the high jump instead of the hoped for 26 and we were back in the pack as the last three events approached. Javelin boys did the business Fortunately our javelin boys did the business. Wes Smith had flown in from Finland at midnight yet still won the B while James Everard nipped past him in the last round to get a good third in the A javelin. The run up for this event at Copthall is so poor that many throwers will not compete there. This together with the heavy rain had an adverse effect on distances. It was going to the wire. The relays would sort it out one way or the other with WGwEL putting out strong teams and the Belgrave men under instructions just to get the batons round - and they did just that. In fact Tim Abeyie (who has left Belgrave and joined WGwEL) just beat Darren Chin to the line in the sprint relay but second was great by us. And so to the final event. New man Chris Minn held third for much of the first leg but faded down the home straight so that Set Osho was having to look for him and the baton in the frenzy that marks the first changeover. Taking over in sixth spot Set gradually powered through moving up to second and being rewarded with a 47.6 split. Next came decathlete Kevin Sempers (who had earlier equalled his pole vault pb) who hung on gamely to again equal his fastest 400 split time. And then to James Ellington. The team managers can remember 14 years ago when they had persuaded John Regis to run his first ever 400 in the long relay. A touch of the deja vu’s here, then, as James strode round the first 200, moved up a place as he put in more effort to 300 and then fought to stay moving as the line approached. By the time he had finished he was barely able to stand. Total exhaustion and the look on his face seemed to say “never again”. But that was what John Regis had said and his split had been the same at 49.4. Will history repeat itself? Actually at that moment not too many people were considering this semi-philosophical question. The relay men had done their jobs. The win, which 5 hours earlier had seemed impossible, had been achieved by a superb team effort. With five pb’s and one A string win backed by eight B string wins this really was a good day for our young squad. items.sum: Pete Mulholland passes on a Running Fitness item revising the M55 1,500m all-time list, in which Belgravians Charlie Dickinson and the late Laurie O’Hara feature.
items.s: Masters Rankings Revisited Pete Mulholland passes on a Running Fitness item revising the M55 1,500m all-time list, in which Belgravians Charlie Dickinson and the late Laurie O’Hara feature. Pete Mulholland informs us that Belgravians Charlie Dickinson and the late Laurie O’Hara feature in a re-shuffling of the M55 1,500m best times ever … and there are still a couple of unanswered question so we’ll delve into the Belgrave archives to see what we can find to back up Charlie’s claim to be British Record holder. From the current edition of Running Fitness The appearance of the masters’ item that appeared in the April edition relating to a British M55 1,500m record being wrongly credited to Harry Tempan, certainly stirred up a hornet’s nest. Maurice Morrell, a fountain of knowledge on the British Masters scene, has been in correspondence with statistician Bob Minting who after much research has arrived at the following conclusion. “All seem agreed that Harry Tempan’s 1981 time of 4 min 32.2 sec had somehow been transposed to 4 min 23.3 sec and/or 4 min 23.2 sec. This means that I have to update the all-time list, the British record and the individual age best at age 56. Harry’s next best time of 4 min 29.95 sec at Brighton in 1984, puts him in ninth place in the all-time list (and is the age 59 best). The next best is currently shown as Steve James with 4 min 25.53 secs, but we know that this is another error and should be 4 min 27.53 secs - which now slots into fifth place). That leaves Charlie Dickinson on top with 4 min 26.5 sec at Tooting Bec in 2003. Also mentioned is the late Laurie O’Hara’s time of 4 min 24.8 sec, which was once shown as a British record. No venue or date was noted and also it did not feature in the top-ten list produced in 2003 by David Burton (the previous BMAF statistician). I can only assume that it was sufficiently uncertain not to be included. Laurie would have had to be satisfied with 4 min 27.4 sec from 1987, which gives him fourth place plus a 4 min 34.8 sec which proves an age 58 best. Unfortunately, I cannot accept Charlie’s time as a British record because we do not have the required documentation to ratify it. It will have to remain a British ‘best’. The next best is John Treadwell’s 4 min 27.08 sec at Bedford in 2000 and as this was at a British Championships I can accept it without documentation as the M55 British record. Running down the updated top ten, the first entry I can find which was done at age 56 is Ian Barnes’ 4 min 28.94 sec at Brighton in 1991. It is not conclusive, but I have no other information that suggests that anyone else (e.g. O’Hara) had a faster time at this specific age. Finally, Steve James did hold the individual age 55 best – but that can now be updated with Charlie’s time, as we know Steve’s had had a couple of seconds knocked off.” 1 C Dickinson 4:26.5 Tooting Bec 30/7/03 2 J Treadwell 4:27:08 Bedford 29/7/00 3 R Phipps 4:27.2 Sutton Coldfield 28/6/00 4 L O'Hara 4:27.4 West London 23/8/87 5 S James 4:27.53 Miyazaki, Japan 16/10/93 6 S Erlam 4:28.9 Wavertree 17/8/96 7 I Barnes 4:28.94 Birmingham 6/7/91 8 B Bullen 4:29.0 Wigan 5/6/88 9 H Tempan 4:29.95 Brighton 28/8/84 10 A Churchill 4:30.1 Watford 4/7/87 55 C Dickinson 4:26.5 Tooting 30/7/03 56 I Barnes 4:28.94 Birmingham 6/7/91 57 R Phipps 4:27.2 Sutton Coldfield 28/6/00 58 L O'Hara 4:34.8 West London 12/8/90 59 H Tempan 4:29.95 Brighton 28/8/84 Pete Mulholland Pete Mulholland Charlie Dickinson Charlie Dickinson M55 1,500m all-time best 4 min 26.5 sec, Tooting Bec 2003 Laurie O’Hara Laurie O’Hara late; M55 1,500m 4 min 27.4 sec 1987 Harry Tempan Harry Tempan Maurice Morrell Maurice Morrell Bob Minting Bob Minting statistician Steve James Steve James David Burton David Burton previous BMAF statistician John Treadwell John Treadwell M55 British 1,500m record 4 min 27.08 sec, Bedford 2000 Ian Barnes Ian Barnes O’Hara O’Hara C Dickinson C Dickinson in M55 1,500m lists J Treadwell J Treadwell in M55 1,500m lists R Phipps R Phipps in M55 1,500m lists L O'Hara L O'Hara in M55 1,500m lists S James S James in M55 1,500m lists S Erlam S Erlam in M55 1,500m lists I Barnes I Barnes in M55 1,500m lists B Bullen B Bullen in M55 1,500m lists H Tempan H Tempan in M55 1,500m lists A Churchill A Churchill in M55 1,500m lists British Championships Tooting Bec Bedford Brighton Sutton Coldfield West London Miyazaki, Japan Wavertree Birmingham Wigan Watford BMAF

items.sum: Look back to 1981: a low ebb at cross country, the London Marathon, John Gladwin, Ernie Obeng, officials' changes and Richard Dorman's walking.
items.s: From The Belgravian Look back to 1981: a low ebb at cross country, the London Marathon, John Gladwin, Ernie Obeng, officials' changes and Richard Dorman's walking. 25 Years Ago – 1981 Things were at a fairly low ebb in 1981. At cross country we had hoped to improve our standing in the North Surrey League but failed to turn out half decent teams – and ended the 1980/81 season being relegated to division two. We did manage to complete teams in each of the male races at the National Cross Country Championships, however, and rounded off the winter season by placing 17th in the Belgrave promoted Haig 12 Stage Relay (including the Southern Championship) – a position with which we were pleased. Thirty-three Belgravians turned out for the 1981 London Marathon, famous for the staged tie for first place between Simonsen (Norway) and Beardsley (USA). First man home for Belgrave was Laurie O’Hara, 333rd in 2:37:53. John Gladwin placed 2nd in the Surrey County Junior CC (leading Belgrave to a team win) – and won our club 7 ½ miles championship – but he was also troubled by injury and spent some time riding a bike to keep fit. Paul Richley won the county Youths’ title. African sprint champion Ernie Obeng had been awarded the Tommy Green Cup for the third successive year. He had been ranked second in the country the previous season with 10.21 for 100 metres. As we geared up for the forthcoming track season Alan Mead stepped down as T&F Secretary (it had been his second stint in this post) and Leo Coy took up the reins to manage our team which was then in Southern League Div. 1. The women’s team were in Southern Women’s League Div. 3. Our leading race walker of the day was Richard Dorman, winner of our 10k track championship and first Belgravian home (7th) in the National 20k at Kenilworth. He was also 6th in the Leicester Mercury 20 miles. items.label: No. 243
items.sum: Stories from the 2006 Flora London Marathon, where Belgrave again won AAA team medals, with first-hand accounts from Belgrave runners.
items.s: Road Running Stories from the 2006 Flora London Marathon, where Belgrave again won AAA team medals, with first-hand accounts from Belgrave runners. Flora London Marathon, 23 April 2006 More Marathon Medals Each year since 2000, with the exception of 2001, we somehow seem to come away from the London Marathon with a set of AAA team medals. Normally it’s the women’s team that do the business and in 2006 they did it again – with the men just outside the frame in 4th – and neither team was boosted by a “superstar”. Here are some of the stories … Visiting the Thistle Hotel to promote sales of his book The 50 Greatest Marathon Races of All Time, Will Cockerell didn't have too much trouble selling copies to Paul Tergat, Khalid Khannouchi and Haile Gebrselassie. But what tickled him most was the fact that they all wanted his autograph! When Geb saw that his own image was on the front cover he was delighted – “Will, you are top man!” Another sale was to Deena Kastor, and remember, this is before the race. Will wrote on the title page, “to Deena, 2:19:37 here we come...” And then at the post race party she told him: “I beat your prediction by one second! But next time could you write something a little faster?” Twelve year-old Krystal Galley was 4th in her section of the mini-marathon ... She felt that she could have done better if she had been more familiar with the course. Having been told by Dad that when she got to Big Ben there was a right turn and then it was not too far to go, it seemed to take a lifetime running down the Embankment with the clock tower always in sight but never, seemingly, getting any nearer! Malachi Byansi (2:38:18) - pictured left by Tim Watt - looked chirpy during the race and later told us: “I have recovered from the marathon after just two days. After 12 months of a painful knee injury, I was happy to feel the running flowing. From the 2nd mile into the race, our group consisted of John Clarke, Warren Lynch and myself with Joachim Wolf 50 yards ahead of us and moving quicker. John was advising me to stop surging; I guess I was running the African way… He suggested an even pace - which I gladly welcomed. The opening splits were: 5:39, 5:43, 5:30, 5:38, 5:32, 5:53. John asked what pace was I going for, and I replied to him that I was looking for 6 mins per mile. Then: 5:53, 5:50, 5:44 and 6:02. After 10 miles I knew I was feeling good but you have to respect the 26.2miles. So I eased down and let the guys go hoping to catch them in the second half of the race. My pace then stayed more or less the same all the way to 18 miles. I was looking forward to the pebbles at Tower Bridge but they never came. I had not realised that the course had changed since I last did it in 2004. My slowest mile was 21 at 6:32. I guess it is psychological because my wheels normally come off at this stage, but once I ingested some energy gels I was fine to carry on. The only thing I can say is that I was too conservative….. next time I will run the African way.” Louise Cooper (3:00:55) – right – was happy at Tower Bridge - but not so delighted at missing a sub 3 hours run by 55 seconds ... “It was all going to plan early on. I think I realised that my 6:40-something miles were creeping closer to 7-somethings, and then I was trying desperately hard to get there, but think I hit the wall with a mile to go - nightmare! It’s been a range of emotions since finishing, sometimes pleased, but more often than not, reflecting over and over again on what I could have done better to get me under three hours. Having done my first London marathon aged 18, and run everyone since (number 13 yesterday), I think I was smiling because I just love the race so much! I couldn't believe how much support for Belgrave there was on route, and I want to thank everyone who gave me a shout. Tom Hadfield (2:39:30) also thanks those who supported him and goes on: “Conditions were absolutely perfect, but I ran a horrid race - started out quite conservatively but felt completely spent by halfway and had nothing in the second half. It was the kind of race that makes you never want to run again. In retrospect I peaked too early - my best races were back in February and it’s all been downhill from there.” A minute came off the previous best set by Lars Rehn (3:26:28). He tells us: “My preparations had not been ideal as I had three weeks off running at the end of March due to a fractured rib that I obtained on a ski holiday. I was on 3:15 pace until 30k, got stomach cramps at 40k and had to stop and stretch. I’m just happy to be able to run a marathon again though, as I have been struggling with injuries since the Berlin Marathon of 2004. I’ve been seeing lots of physiotherapists, sports doctors, podiatrists, biomechanical lecturer, spinal surgeons etc., and finally I found out that the cause of my problems are a disc prolapse in my lower back. I might need surgery as I got sciatic pain, does anyone know who might have experience with micro discectomy ? After recovering next couple of weeks, I hope to do some 5 and 10k races over the summer. Thanks to David Lucas for coaching us on Tuesday nights.” It was a case of “getting the feel of the occasion” and learning the route for Simon Jones (2:33:04) ... A personal record came from John Clarke (2:30:31), our first man home: “Thanks for the support on Sunday which resulted in a PB by just under 5 minutes and also 13 minutes quicker than my last London outing in 2004. The race went perfectly for the first half with my plan for a late 2:28/2:29 clocking being bang on. However, for some reason miles 18-20 saw me hit a big bad patch causing me to lose the bunch I was running with and making my chances for the last miles look pretty bleak. The training I have done did however pay dividends as I managed to claw it back and get back on course, but this extra effort ultimately caught up with me over the last mile and a half meaning that I just missed my target time. Can’t complain though as it could have been much worse and the improvements continue to come. Also, lessons have been learned that will be carried into my next marathon in the Autumn.” Lee Greatorex ran with the intention of going half distance and ran three personal bests along the way - 10km in 33:45, 10 miles in 55:05 and the Half Marathon in 72:58. Nikki Neal (2:54:19) had a fabulous run and may have broken the Channel Islands record ... Warren Lynch, on schedule for 2:30, became too ill to continue at 17 miles. Tim Weeks had a torrid time – well it might have been better if he’d done some training. It all started out ok with an initial 10k split of 39:19. Even his second one wasn’t too bad – 40:43. But then it all fell apart with a 46:42 and finally 80:02 – by which time he was alternately walking to one lamp post and running the next two. He says he must have looked bad because little kids were running out into the road to feed him jelly babies! items.sum: Eric Hall's tribute to race walker George Beecham, recalling their friendly rivalry since a six-miles-in-the-hour walk at Wimbledon in 1950 and George's long walking and charity career.
items.s: Long Standing Partnership! Eric Hall's tribute to race walker George Beecham, recalling their friendly rivalry since a six-miles-in-the-hour walk at Wimbledon in 1950 and George's long walking and charity career. On 29th April 1950 two young men toed the line at Wimbledon both hoping to walk six miles in the hour for the recently introduced RWA badge. The result shows they both gained the award and that George Beecham had the upper hand finishing second well inside sixty minutes. George joined Belgrave at the instigation of Ron Durbin, a Club runner. To gain some early experience he had “strolled” home to Sutton from Brighton! Shortly after that first race the two young men struck up a friendly rivalry which saw them give the Club handicapper, Bill True, a torrid time. In those days the Club had a series of 2 mile handicaps at monthly intervals. Being novices the pair started from a limit mark of around 700 yards on Harry Churcher, holder of the world five mile record. For almost two seasons they played Box and Cox by taking turns in hard fought races to win prizes and find their level. By this time, in the wider walking world, they were making names for themselves in the Open races, with George winning the Met. Police Open 7 mile handicap, and establishing themselves in the Club B team, and, finally by 1954, the A team. George had by this time tackled some of the longer events with success. This progress was to continue and even today George’s stamina is legendary. He tackled both the London to Brighton walk and the very stiff Hastings to Brighton 14 times, with an individual win in the latter, plus numerous team successes in both events. A vital member of many National teams he has the unique distinction of eight successive team wins for the Nijmegen Shield. This was awarded to the first team to finish all eight members in the National 20 mile championship. That record was achieved in the glory days of Belgrave walkers when you almost had to be an international to get in the team. His 4th place in the National 50 kms championship, at Preston, in 1957 gained him an international vest in Belgium that year where he finished 3rd. Having accompanied the two Wilson brothers on London to Brighton and back races (104 miles) George also completed 100 miles in 24 hours in 1981 to gain the prestigious Centurion award. Never one to rest on his laurels George became very involved in charity work on Canvey Island. As a long time sufferer from asthma he set out to raise funds for a connected charity. In addition he has been a member of the local sports council for many years receiving an award for his efforts. Another award, of which he is rightly very proud, is a Silver Medal from the RNLI for his work on their behalf. As part of his fund raising activities he has completed 11 London marathons walking all the way with times well under 6 hours on most occasions. He uses this event to warm up for his annual trip to Nijmegen where he walks 50kms on each of 4 successive days. For this he holds a set of 15 medals – which if awarded to a Dutch serviceman can be worn as a military decoration. He will soon be bidding for a 16th! All this from a stroll home from Brighton and a successful attempt to gain a six miles in the hour badge. Not finished yet George renewed his rivalry with his opponent since 1950 on the 30th April 2006. This time round George finished behind his rival, which was not so surprising as he had been up early to set up the course and generally assist in the organisation of the day. During the walk it became evident that George is well known on Canvey and he is particularly proud of having introduced Dean Macey to athletics through his coaching nights at the local track. In case you wonder what happened to George’s rival - well he writes the occasional piece for the Belgravian! items.s: It’s all to play for in the BAL Premiership Division Overview of the British Athletics League Premiership at halfway, with Belgrave level on league points with Woodford Green after Birchfield's match-two score was corrected, and the league standings. Track & Field At the halfway stage of the 2006 season and going into match three at Birmingham on July 1st, Woodford Green wEL and Belgrave are virtually neck and neck - both on 15 league points but the Essex club having a 25.5 match point advantage. At the second match at Manchester a weakened Belgrave squad wound up third with the result that the Essex based team had an advantage of one league point overall. But rumblings among team managers resulted in Birchfield’s team being scrutinised a little more closely – and it became obvious that due to a misunderstanding with the rules, they had fielded too many foreign and higher-claim athletes. The match was subsequently rescored with a few of their guys having been removed from the results and as a result, in match two, Birchfield slipped to 6th and Belgrave moved up to 2nd. Woodford Green wEL and Belgrave now have one win and one second place apiece. Below we give you the second match report and results as they were immediately after the event, together with the amended team result. items.sum: Bill Laws's report on British Athletics League Premiership Match Two at Manchester Sport City on 6 May 2006, where Belgrave placed third (second in the corrected team result), with Belgrave results.
items.s: We live to fight again Bill Laws's report on British Athletics League Premiership Match Two at Manchester Sport City on 6 May 2006, where Belgrave placed third (second in the corrected team result), with Belgrave results. Premiership Division, Match Two, Manchester Sport City, 6 May 2006. We live to fight again Last year our match at Manchester proved to be our nemesis, writes Bill Laws. This year’s visit had been viewed with trepidation, especially as England’s footballers were playing Jamaica at Old Trafford just eight miles away. Travel was bound to be difficult and could we get the team there in one piece? Fourteen athletes had to be replaced At the beginning of the week the turnout looked good enough to continue our winning ways but by the end of the week overseas duties and injuries meant that half our winning match one team were missing. Fourteen athletes had to be replaced. Some places could not be filled but nonetheless we were rewarded with some splendid performances. Joe didn’t disappoint Another early start – to fit in the double fixture with the UKWAL Div 1 fixture – saw our single vaulter, junior Joe Ive, determined to make up for his match one hiccup. And he didn’t disappoint. In swirling conditions he equalled his recent 5.00m pb and narrowly failed the Beijing qualifying height of 5.15m to gain a fine second place. Meanwhile there was controversy in the discus as the out of stadium field was declared to be too sloping to qualify for legal marks. The circle, too, had been cast just two days earlier and had a ridge in it. All this made Woodford’s Emeka Udechuku’s winning distance even more impressive. Leith Marar improved on his match one distance but in a close battle he finished below target while Mark Allen, competing for the first time for Belgrave in the discus, was also a bit below par. But the track started with a bang, as in the A 400 hurdles Ryan Dinham ran his first sub 51sec clocking from an outside lane to just miss out on first spot and the B race saw the first appearance in this event for Belgrave of another young athlete Chris Minn who too was rewarded with a pb. Graeme jumps the field This was quickly followed by some exciting tactical 800m races. In the first, Graeme Oudney had only one race plan – to go from 300m. And he did! A slow first lap of 60sec saw the field gather ready for a sprint finish but they were all surprised as Graeme jumped at 500m and quickly opened a 25m gap which even the fastest sprinters could not pull back. Negative splits are not unusual but to run the second lap in 52 secs which was a huge 7 seconds faster than the first, is pretty rare. The B 800 was a mirror image of the first but on this occasion Jonathan Blackledge got boxed down the back straight and by the time he had extricated himself in the home straight it was too late to catch the leaders. But another negative split. Welcome back Wade And the sprints that followed continued the momentum with Wade Bennett Jackson making a welcome season’s debut after injury, claiming a fine 3rd in the A 100m followed by a second placing in the B race for Darren Chin. It was unfortunate that for both races the electric timing failed and the track judges had to decide the positions. Wade was clearly second in the unbiased eyes of the Belgrave supporters. Later Darren Chin was to win the B 200m from lane 1 in a big season’s best after Jason Hussain had disappointed in the A race, running nearly a second slower than his previous week’s Inter-Counties time. We were sacrificing big points All we can say about the steeplechase is that with only one entry we were sacrificing big points. Nevertheless veteran Paul Beaumont’s 4 points were better than none. The flat 400 was another event where our missing specialists made point scoring difficult. Ryan Dinham was feeling the effects of his earlier event but gave 110%, as too did Ian Deeth who has returned to the team after a five year absence. But there were not enough points here for us to advance. And in the 1500m Richard Ward was both our only middle distance man from match one and our only entry in this event. By now too many points had been uncontested and when the scores were announced late afternoon, Belgrave had drifted back from 1st to third spot with Birchfield just ahead of WGwEL. Our hope now was that Birchfield would push WGwEL into second spot so we could end the match with equal league points. But it was not to be. Non specialists William Sharman and James Everard performed well in the high jump but the competition was so classy that they made little impression on the points. A similar scenario unfolded in the javelin where both James Everard and Wes Smith threw further than in match one but were rewarded with fewer points. James also got a mark in the triple jump where Farel Mepandy bettered 15m to gain a fine second spot in the A event. Meanwhile Mark Allen and Chris Gearing redressed the balance with good points in the shot when a drop to fourth team spot appeared a possibility. Hurdlers come up trumps again A glimmer of hope was provided when William Sharman squeezed a sprint hurdles victory into a huge headwind followed by a clear second victory from Dominic Girdler in the B event. William was to be rewarded with an invitation to the following Sunday’s Gateshead Grand Prix. Simon Jones was a welcome debutant in the 5000 and was to see one of Birchfield’s many Kenyan athletes run a non-scoring 13:48 time trial. Backed by the ubiquitous Will Cockerell we were just holding on to third spot. Will has been compiling statistics on the Bels’ 5000 BAL representatives and appears to have proved he has competed twice as many times as his nearest rival. No doubt a bit more of that in “Skippers Corner” before long! So to the relays Well aware that a dropped baton could change the placings of most of the teams, the Belgrave squad played it safe and were only headed by the WGwEL quartet who won by virtue of some very slick baton changing. With the long relay to go we were still aware that a baton infringement could change the final result. And then, with 15 minutes to the start, Jason Hussain was unwell and to his great credit Darren Chin stepped in to fill the breach. How he managed to sprint down the home straight only he knows but he gave Graeme Oudney a sniff of gaining a place, Graeme responded with the fastest split of the day but again our lack of specialist one lappers was to prove our undoing. But we had held on to third match place and we live to fight again in Birmingham in four weeks time. It was a long drive home through throngs of football supporters, celebrating a 6-0 win over Jamaica. items.s: The win streak goes on Report and results from UK Women's Athletics League Division Three Match One at Bedford on 3 June 2006, won by Belgrave, with Janine Whitlock setting a division pole vault record. UK Women’s Athletics League Division Three, Match One, Bedford, 3 June 2006. The win streak goes on Yep! Unbeaten in 2005 and winners of the opening UKWAL match in 2006, the quest for promotion goes on, but this was no easy match. Marshall Milton Keynes AC made a great fight of it and Blackheath & Bromley Harriers, promoted with the Belles at the end of 2005, will be sure to have a say in the matter before this season is over. Points were hard to come by but five individual winners tipped the balance our way with the pole vault our top event thanks to Janine Whitlock and Jenny Searle. Janine needed three tries at 4.15m but her eventual clearance was a new Division Three record and only 5cm shy of the overall league record held by ... Janine herself, set seven years ago when she competed for Trafford AC. Hannah Stares was a double winner – taking both hurdle races and prepared to tackle whatever the team managers threw her way. Our other win came from none other than Michelle Nestor – 11.06m in the triple jump – and as we’ve said before, goodness knows what she’d do if she ever trained. Sarah Wellstead scored well in the A strings of the horizontal jumps – two second places to her – and it was good to see Diana Holden in the team and scoring equally well in the A hammer and B discus where U20 Jade Lally maintained her consistent 2006 series of throws well over 40 metres to place second in the A event. Great start then - and we look forward to more of the same at Coventry on July 2nd. 100m: 5 J Culley 12.41w/2.9; 5 K Euridge 13.8/1.8. 200m: 4 J Culley 25.27w/3.2; 5 C Foster 26.55/1.3. 400m: 5 C Robinson 58.65; 5 S Gailey 62.04. 800m: 3 C Robinson 2:13.73; 3 C Foster 2:21.39. 1500m: 3 C Pryson 4:39.04; 2 C Shanklyn 4:42.25. 3000m: 5 S Murphy 10:41.83; 5 L Cooper 11:46.14. 100mH: 1 H Stares 14.53w/2.3; 3 C Bertram 18.58w/2.3. 400mH: H Stares 61.11; 4 V Goodwin 73.07. items.sum: Report and results from the Horwich Carnival 5km incorporating the AAA 5km Championship, where Belgrave won the AAA team gold medals after placing second to Birchfield in the open team race.
items.s: Roads still paved with gold Report and results from the Horwich Carnival 5km incorporating the AAA 5km Championship, where Belgrave won the AAA team gold medals after placing second to Birchfield in the open team race. Road Running Horwich Carnival 5km inc. AAA Championship Roads still paved with gold The AAA 5km Championship is only in its second year and on each occasion it has been held as part of the delightful Horwich Carnival Races – a meeting that also takes in the BMAF 5km Championship, the conclusion of the Countryside Tour of Horwich & Rivington, various cycle races including the British National Elite Men’s Circuit Championship and the Carnival Parade complete with beauty queen and the famous Horwich RMI Clog Dancers – all on the same circuit (though not, thankfully, at the same time). Local man Paul Freary was in action early, figuring that we had enough fire power in the senior men’s race to do without him and electing to run as a Master. He tucked into the slipstream of Blackheath & Bromley’s Dave Taylor who set a ferocious pace and the two were clear of the field after one lap. But there were two more circuits to go and our man was unable to hang on to Taylor who went on to set an astounding veteran time of 14:38. Paul won the M35 category but didn’t want to make too much of that as two, albeit outstanding, M40s were ahead of him by the time the line was reached. Charlie Dickinson came through as the race progressed - eventually just missing out on M50 medals - while the team race went to our local rivals Herne Hill, headed by Roger Alsop. In the AAA Championship race Birchfield’s men tore away from the start with only Chris Davies (Telford) and Peter Riley (Leigh) getting anywhere near them. But Mark Miles worked hard throughout the race and his final placing of 5th (3rd in the AAA Championship) is a pleasure to record. He was a little disappointed with the time – but what a way to come back in his first race after a long lay-off. To say that we are thrilled to have him back in the team is an understatement. Simon Jones had reported a minor calf problem but his solid run as tenth Briton was key to our team placing while it was great to see “Wardy” mixing road success with speedy track runs. Do you know that as a result of his glandular fever and two years of below par results – Richard Ward is now operating at 3:48 1500m level on 30 miles per week? In 2005 we missed out on the AAA team title by the narrowest of margins, having equalled Salford’s score but got our last scoring man home behind theirs; even that situation had only been reached after some overseas competitors were removed from the scoring (without which we would have won) while others (Birchfield’s African stars) were not. The intervening year had seen us propose that AAA team places should be calculated on accumulated times, therefore obviating the need to decide who should be removed from the scoring and who shouldn’t – and this has been accepted as the rule for 2006 onwards. Another complicating feature of these events is the fact that for an overseas athlete to win a AAA individual medal he or she must have been resident in the UK for nine months - thus ruling out the Birchfield guys - while to score for a UK club an overseas athlete only has to be resident for two months. Even getting our first three home onto the scoring sheet had not been without problems as Richard Ward had been left off the result and our Team Manager, ensconced in the warmth of the Cafe Marina and doing justice to a post-race minted lamb pie with brown sauce, was dragged off to Race HQ to clear things up after a phone call from Richard outlined the potential setback. Suffice it to say that at the conclusion of the race we were resigned to the fact that we had placed second team on the day to the awesome onslaught of Birchfield’s men, bolstering ourselves with the thought that we were, at least, first “British” team. We went along to the presentation to receive our second set of silver medals, only to fine that Birchfield, though winning the Open Race, were not included in the Championship event. The golden booty was ours. items.h: William Sharman - Athlete of the month
items.sum: News item, from the UKA website, on William Sharman being named the first UK Challenge Athlete of the Month for May 2006.
items.s: William Sharman - Athlete of the month News item, from the UKA website, on William Sharman being named the first UK Challenge Athlete of the Month for May 2006. News From the UKA Website. William Sharman has been named the first UK Challenge Athlete of the Month winner, for his performances during May. The Belgrave Harrier scored a total of 375 points, thanks to a 13.85w 110 hurdles victory in the Inter Counties Championships at Bedford and a 14.22 win in the first round of the British League matches at Hendon. The 13.85 win in Bedford netted him 201 points while the 14.22 earned him another 174 and so securing the award along with the accompanying prize of a Polar Heart Rate monitor. Sharman also won the British Universities 110m hurdles in May. While he is primarily a hurdler (fourth in last year’s European U23 Championships), he is also one of the country’s top multi-eventers. The 21 year-old topped the UK Decathlon rankings in 2005 with a score of 7384 points, before deciding to focus on sprint hurdles. items.label: No. 244
items.h: Greg Billington - a double win in Europe
items.sum: News item on Greg Billington's 1500m and 3000m double at the DODDS European Championships in Wiesbaden on 19-20 May 2006.
items.s: Greg Billington - a double win in Europe News item on Greg Billington's 1500m and 3000m double at the DODDS European Championships in Wiesbaden on 19-20 May 2006. May 19-20. In Wiesbaden, Germany, Greg Billington – not quite 17 but competing in under 19 competition – won a DODDS European Championships (Department of Defense American Schools) double at 1500m and 3000m in poor conditions and with tactical flair. Greg and coach Mick Graham have been working on “change of pace” and in the 1500m the Belgrave man was able to turn on a 43 second last 300 for the win in 4:01. In an all-out run he should go well under 4 minutes. For the 3000m the weather conditions were horrendous with the track being closed due to lightning as the runners were ready to start. When the runners were finally allowed to begin the race, they were soaked and cold and the track was covered with lakes. It was another cat and mouse race and this time Greg hit the accelerator with 500m to go, covering the final lap in 61.0 seconds. His winning time was 8:58. Since then Greg has recorded an 8:38 but has been nowhere near stretched yet and Mick expects him to go under 15 minutes for 5k whenever he gets the chance. He was 15:25 last year and has come on considerably since then – thanks to Mick and his own hard work. Plans for the summer include the AAA U20 5000m and some training sessions with Tom Osment’s group which includes other outstanding young Belgravians Joe van der Toorn and Phil Wicks. items.sum: Extracts from The Belgravian of 1931 on Arthur Penny's club record win in the 3 Miles Championship for the Griffin Cup, T.H. Scrimshaw at the AAA Championships and walker Tommy Green, with modern notes.
items.s: From The Belgravian – 75 Years Ago – 1931 Extracts from The Belgravian of 1931 on Arthur Penny's club record win in the 3 Miles Championship for the Griffin Cup, T.H. Scrimshaw at the AAA Championships and walker Tommy Green, with modern notes. From The Belgravian 75 Years Ago – 1931 June 24th – The chief event of the evening was the 3 Miles Championship for “The Griffin Cup.” Unfortunately Arthur Allum, the holder, was unable to compete due to ankle trouble, sustained at the end of the Winter season. Wally Bayliss led the field in the early stages of the race, but was displaced after a while by Arthur Penny, closely followed by Jack Flower. It was obvious that the championship was going to resolve itself into a struggle between the two last named and this proved to be the case. Over the last lap Arthur drew away, and although Jack seemed to gain a little in the last fifty yards, Penny won by a few yards in the Club record time of 15min. 6sec. C.T. Carter ran well to finish third and would have been much nearer the leaders but for an attack of “stitch” over the last two laps. He should show considerable improvement over the country this coming season. Fourth came H.E. Footer and fifth N. Dewberry. The 2006 edition of this club championship race – for the very same “Griffin Cup” – will take place at Battersea Park on Wednesday 19th July. July 3rd and 4th. – A.A.A. Championships. T.H. Scrimshaw distinguished himself by running second in his heat and fourth in the final, with T. Hampson, S. Townend and Dr. Peltzer in front of him. Truly remarkable running for a lad not yet twenty-one. With the walkers. We are very glad to see Tommy Green out again, and although he is not yet his old self, he has already been responsible for some very fine performances. Best of these, perhaps, was to beat T. Lloyd Johnson, the National 20 miles and 50 kilometres champion, in a 25 miles race at Manchester. Tommy was recovering from the misfortune of losing a thumb in the course of his work at the railway works at Eastleigh. He went on to win the Olympic 50 kilometres Walk at Los Angeles in 1932. items.sum: News item on Belgrave middle-distance runners at the BMC Nike Grand Prix at Watford on 10 June 2006.
items.s: Middle Distance Mayhem News item on Belgrave middle-distance runners at the BMC Nike Grand Prix at Watford on 10 June 2006. Sat 10 Jun. Junior Kris Gauson blasted to a 1:50.45 800m win at the BMC Nike GP at Watford on Saturday night, sticking close to the pacemaker during the first lap and then striking out alone for a clear victory in a huge personal best. Stephen Sharp, back after a knee niggle and then a tumble in the previous Wednesday’s 3000m at St. Mary’s Twickenham, ran to 3:45.33 in the A 1500m, moving him to number three on our 2006 rankings behind Messrs. Speaight and Bayley. The B race saw an almighty tear-up between Phil Wicks, Richard Ward and Jonathan Blackledge. Jonathan stayed closest to the pacemaker with Richard towards the back of the field over the initial lap. Phil took a battering in the middle of the race, drifting back and then working his way forward again. Over the final circuit a powerful surge down the back straight saw Phil moving forward fast, followed by Richard. Both managed to pass Jonathan as all three went well under 3:50. Personal records came from Phil and Jonathan and it was a real treat to see Richard getting right back to his old form. Darren Gauson was an interested spectator at Watford on this occasion. He’s over his quad problem now and looks forward to a couple of weeks at altitude before returning to competition. Keeping an eye on the emerging talent, Spencer Barden, UKA’s Senior Co-ordinator for Endurance, looked in fine fettle. He declared that he’s training - and looking forward to racing in the Corporate Challenge in a few weeks time.
